name: ICU4X
baseline: ICU4C (line break and word break iterators)
workload: Line and word segmentation (UAX #14 and UAX #29) of non-complex-script text and of Chinese text, ICU4X segmenter versus ICU4C equivalents.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: 'line and word segmenters are 19.1% and 52.2% faster in non-complex scripts and 46.9% and 32.1% faster in Chinese than the equivalents in ICU4C, respectively' (ICU4X 1.2 announcement on the Unicode blog).
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; maintained by the Unicode Consortium
tradeoffs: Implemented in Rust with Diplomat-generated C and C++ headers (ffi/capi), so callable from C++ but needs a Rust-built library. Design goals are small, modular code and pluggable locale data. The segmenter covers grapheme, word, sentence and line breaking; normalizer, collator and other components also exist. The speed claim found concerns only the segmenter.
caveats: The percentages appear only in a web-search result snippet of blog.unicode.org (ICU4X 1.2 announcement); that site and the numbers could not be opened from this environment (egress blocked), and the GitHub repo, the 1.2.0 release page and issue #66 carry no ICU4C comparison numbers (components/segmenter/benches/bench.rs exists but is Rust-only). Test data, hardware, compiler and ICU4C version are unknown, and the 2023 numbers may be stale. A verifier with blog access should confirm the quote. Category fit is marginal: Unicode segmentation, not shaping or rasterization. Rust implementation, with C++ bindings, not a native C++ library.
found_via: WebSearch 'ICU4X benchmark faster than ICU4C normalizer OR segmenter OR collator OR "case mapping" performance numbers' (snippet from blog.unicode.org 2023/04 ICU4X 1.2 post); repo page, segmenter and ffi/capi directories and commits page opened on github.com.

name: kb_text_shape
baseline: HarfBuzz
workload: OpenType text segmentation and shaping; the author's claimed run used HarfBuzz's own test suite extended with the author's tests, while the HarfBuzz maintainer's run used Roboto-Regular (paragraphs and single words), Amiri-Regular (Arabic), Gulzar-Regular (Urdu and English) and NotoSansDevanagari-Regular (Hindi words).
claimed_speedup: No speedup verified. The kb repo README and header carry no benchmark numbers. The page at benchmark_url, a HarfBuzz maintainer's comparison, shows kb slower than HarfBuzz: HarfBuzz 2.9x faster on Roboto-Regular paragraph text, 3.3x faster word by word, kb about 20% slower on Amiri-Regular, kb 6.6x slower on Gulzar-Regular Urdu, kb 160x slower on Gulzar-Regular English text, kb 2x slower on NotoSansDevanagari-Regular, and kb needs 40x to 760x more time to load a font. See caveats for the author's own opposite claim, which this session could not open.
compiler_and_flags: Author's claim only (not opened): clang 20 on Linux, flags not stated. HarfBuzz maintainer run: compiler and flags not stated.
hardware: Author's claim only (not opened): Ryzen 9 5900HX. HarfBuzz maintainer run: CPU not stated.
tradeoffs: Single-header C/C++ library (about 22k lines at announcement; header is v2.28e) that bundles Unicode segmentation and OpenType shaping with no dependencies. README says it does not handle rasterization, paragraph layout or system font loading. The header states it gives NO SECURITY GUARANTEE and must not be used on untrusted font files. HarfBuzz maintainer notes it copies whole font files into memory and lacks cluster information needed for cursor positioning, selection and editing.
caveats: Disputed speed claim, kept so the orchestrator can decide. A WebSearch result snippet attributed to the author (X post and developer blog, both unreachable here: x.com and handmade.network are blocked) says kb is on average 4.5x faster than HarfBuzz at shaping, measured on HarfBuzz's test suite extended with the author's own tests, Ryzen 9 5900HX, clang 20, Linux. The number 4.5x was not seen on any page opened this session. The only opened comparison, written by the HarfBuzz maintainer (a party with an interest in the result) in July 2025 against an early release, found kb slower on every listed font and workload, with crashes in some test suites. Later kb releases (v2.28e now, 'Faster GSUB and GPOS feature culling' in the v2.06 changelog) may have changed this. The maintainer's discussion says HarfBuzz later added a kb backend to its own perf benchmark suite; running that suite would settle it. Best treated as reference or a flagged entry, not a verified win.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN text shaping library faster than HarfBuzz' surfaced the thread 'Kb_text_shape: Harfbuzz like single file C/C++ text shaping library' (item 46750420); a second WebSearch 'kb_text_shape benchmark vs HarfBuzz shaping speed single-header' surfaced the claim snippet and the HarfBuzz discussion 5375.

name: msdfgl
baseline: msdfgen (Chlumsky's CPU multi-channel signed distance field generator, single-threaded and OpenMP builds); incumbent for MSDF font atlas generation, not one of HarfBuzz or FreeType
workload: Generating an MSDF texture for ASCII characters 0-127 of the font DejaVu Sans at four scale factors (1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0), mean of 100 runs, OpenGL context creation and destruction time and shader compilation excluded.
claimed_speedup: Chart numbers in README image (msdfgl vs msdfgen vs msdfgen with OpenMP): scale 1.0 0.0081 s vs 0.4890 s vs 0.1334 s; scale 2.0 0.0164 s vs 1.9390 s vs 0.5182 s; scale 4.0 0.0645 s vs 7.7407 s vs 1.9939 s; scale 8.0 0.2345 s vs 31.0000 s vs 8.0000 s (the two msdfgen values at 8.0 were extrapolated by the author). Ratios (derived from page data): about 60x, 118x, 120x and 132x faster than single-threaded msdfgen, and about 16x, 32x, 31x and 34x faster than OpenMP msdfgen.
hardware: Core i7 8550m (as written in README) with Intel UHD Graphics 620, Debian Linux
tradeoffs: GPU implementation written from scratch in C; needs an OpenGL 3.3 core or OpenGL ES 3.2 context. The algorithm was reworked to run in shaders: no cubic Bezier segments (so CFF/PostScript-flavoured OpenType outlines are not handled), constant memory, no pointers. Shader compilation takes about one second once. Output is a ready-to-use GPU atlas and index texture, so no upload step.
caveats: First-party benchmark on one weak integrated GPU and one laptop CPU; the benchmark code, compiler and flags for msdfgen and msdfgl are not given. The README says the msdfgen timing excludes transferring bitmaps to a texture whereas msdfgl's includes being render-ready. Largest-scale msdfgen points are extrapolated, not measured. Image quality parity with msdfgen (error correction, cubic segments) is not evaluated. Baseline is msdfgen, not FreeType or HarfBuzz, and the speedup is GPU versus CPU rather than a like-for-like algorithm win. Numbers were read from the chart image /img/benchmarks.png in the README (labels printed on the bars).
found_via: WebFetch github.com/topics/msdf; README and img/benchmarks.png fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com and the chart viewed; commits page opened.

name: Parley
baseline: cosmic-text 0.19.0 (pop-os/cosmic-text), the other Rust rich-text shaping and layout library; both sit on HarfRust shaping
workload: Shaping and laying out text in six corpora (Latin, pure-RTL Arabic, bidirectional Arabic plus Latin, CJK, ZWJ emoji, Devanagari) at paragraph and 10,000-line document scale with warm and cold caches (parley 0.11.1 vs cosmic-text 0.19.0); a second, terminal workload measured with criterion.
claimed_speedup: flui PR 1276 (merged 2026-09-23): 'parley wins on timing across all six corpora (2.4x-8.4x faster)', final figures 2.4x-9.0x faster after methodology corrections, and 1.2x-4.2x less memory. massive PR 154 (merged 2026-09-15, criterion, M-series Mac, bundled JetBrains Mono 13 px): parley wins full mixed line (~4.8x), full-screen throughput (~2x) and fallback stress (~2.7x); cosmic-text wins the single-cluster hot path (~16%) and cold FontSystem construction (~600x).
hardware: PR 1276: 'an otherwise-idle machine' (no CPU model); PR 154: 'M-series Mac'
tradeoffs: Rust-only (not callable from C++ without bindings). Depends on Fontique, HarfRust, Skrifa and ICU4X. Larger binary than fontdue-style rasterizers (a separate PR measured +40% binary size when replacing fontdue with parley and swash). cosmic-text starts faster cold (FontSystem construction) and wins the single-cluster hot path.
caveats: Third-party measurements, both from downstream projects' own research PRs, not from the Parley project and not peer reviewed. PR 1276 is co-authored with an AI assistant, uses a custom harness (not criterion), states no CPU or rustc flags, and went through two rounds of self-correction (an O(n squared) cost in parley's single-Layout approach and a memory-retention asymmetry); its raw data sits in tools/text-spike/ of the flui repo and was not opened. flui issue 931 relays an unverified downstream report that floem found parley '93% slower on Arabic wrap' and says not to cite it as settled. A bevy issue (21765) has only qualitative 'significantly better' remarks. Baseline is cosmic-text, not HarfBuzz or FreeType. Not on the known list.
found_via: WebSearch 'text layout benchmark cosmic-text parley swash skrifa Pango comparison results performance'; flui PR 1276, flui issue 931, massive PR 154, bevy issue 21765, linebender/parley README and commits page read

name: rustybuzz-wasm
language: Rust (compiled to WebAssembly, driven from NodeJS)
baseline: harfbuzzjs (HarfBuzz compiled to WebAssembly, driven from NodeJS); also the HarfBuzz command-line tools spawned per line, opentype.js and fontkit
workload: Shaping 100 lines of text with 100 words per line (65,732 Unicode code units), measured as items per second from NodeJS; several runs in randomized order.
claimed_speedup: README prose: 'rustybuzz-wasm would appear to be 1.5 times faster than harfbuzzjs'. Table in the introduction: rustybuzz_wasm_rusty_shaping 218,840 Hz vs harfbuzzjs_shaping 176,392 Hz (about 1.24x, derived from page data); bar-chart rows 220,399 Hz vs 143,434 Hz (about 1.54x, derived from page data). The same tables show 'over 12 times' against the HarfBuzz command line (harfbuzz_shaping 17,553 Hz), which the author says is dominated by spawning one process per line and re-reading fonts and 'does not tell you how fast HarfBuzz itself is'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark; README says to build with 'wasm-pack build --target nodejs' (release) because debug builds are orders of magnitude slower. Node.js version not stated.
hardware: '2015 customer grade, not fast, not new, not fancy laptop' (no CPU model)
tradeoffs: Not feature-complete with rustybuzz: values cross the WASM boundary as JSON and hex-encoded strings; the README says harfbuzzjs does not allow arbitrarily long lines and does not support font features, and that rustybuzz-wasm is not feature-complete with rustybuzz yet. The repo also does SVG glyph rendering via ttf-parser and line wrapping via textwrap. Needs a Rust toolchain and wasm-pack to build; WASM artifacts are committed and may be unoptimized. Not callable from C++.
caveats: Weak evidence: the benchmark code is not in this repo (README links loveencounterflow/hengist, dev/glyphshapes-and-typesetting-with-harfbuzz/src/textshaping.benchmarks.coffee; that file was not opened). No CPU, Node version or font file is given. The win over the nearest comparable baseline (harfbuzzjs) is only about 1.2x to 1.5x; the 12x to 17x figures are against a per-line process-spawning command-line setup and say nothing about HarfBuzz itself. The LICENSE file contains the placeholder text 'the liecense goes here', so no license is granted (rustybuzz itself is MIT). Last commit February 2022, and the README says it is a fragmentary work in progress. Separately, HarfBuzz's maintainer reports (harfbuzz/harfrust discussion 257, 2025-09-10) that the Rust port HarfRust is within about 25% of, i.e. slower than, native HarfBuzz, so this is a WASM-versus-WASM result only.
found_via: WebSearch 'harfrust OR rustybuzz benchmark vs HarfBuzz shaping speed results table' surfaced the repo; README and LICENSE read via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com

name: sigilbuzz
baseline: rustybuzz (Rust port of HarfBuzz); HarfBuzz itself is not measured
workload: Shaping the same 200-codepoint string per script through sigilbuzz and rustybuzz back to back (Latin Open Sans with liga and kern, Arabic Amiri, Devanagari Noto, Khmer Noto, Hebrew Noto), Criterion medians from the 0.6.0 release.
claimed_speedup: Faster than rustybuzz on two of five scripts: Latin 11.39 us vs 15.03 us (page ratio 0.76x, about 1.32x faster, derived from page data) and Hebrew 10.99 us vs 17.28 us (page ratio 0.64x, about 1.57x faster, derived from page data). Slower on the other three: Arabic 290 us vs 108 us (2.70x slower), Devanagari 419 us vs 85.8 us (4.89x slower), Khmer 91.6 us vs 49.0 us (1.87x slower).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench with Criterion; rustc version and profile flags not stated
hardware: maintainer's macOS arm64 workstation; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Pure Rust core (no_std, no runtime dependencies, deterministic output). C and C++ callers go through the sigilbuzz-capi crate, which exports HarfBuzz hb_* symbols so it can be linked in place of libharfbuzz. Pre-1.0 API, no bug-for-bug compatibility with older HarfBuzz. Also ships a subsetter, WOFF/WOFF2 wrap and unwrap, UAX 14 line breaking, hyphenation, a CPU rasterizer and a Slug-style GPU outline encoder.
caveats: Baseline is rustybuzz, not HarfBuzz or FreeType; the benchmark never runs the sigilbuzz C API against libharfbuzz. rustybuzz's own README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harfbuzz/rustybuzz/main/README.md) says it is 1.5-2x slower than HarfBuzz and recommends HarfRust instead, so nothing here shows sigilbuzz beating HarfBuzz. The win is mixed: it loses to rustybuzz on Arabic, Devanagari and Khmer by 1.9x to 4.9x. Numbers are first-party, from one unnamed Apple arm64 machine, one 200-codepoint input per script; the repo is about one day old with 0 stars. Kept only as a registry-found C-callable HarfBuzz alternative with a published, honest comparison; expect a keep-and-document decision at best.
found_via: crates.io API query q=harfbuzz (sigilbuzz-capi, 'HarfBuzz-symbol-compatible C API ... Drop-in -lharfbuzz replacement'), then github.com/Oneiriq/sigilbuzz README and docs/PERFORMANCE.md

name: SixLabors.Fonts
baseline: HarfBuzz via HarfBuzzSharp 14.2.1.1 (native HarfBuzz called from .NET, single-run text shaping)
workload: End-to-end shaping of one short text run per script (Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, Thai, Hangul, Devanagari, Khmer, Myanmar, Myanmar Zawgyi, Balinese), same font file bytes on both sides, BenchmarkDotNet on .NET 10.
claimed_speedup: Release post for Fonts 3.1.0, as quoted by a search-result snippet: on .NET 10 it wins three of the ten scripts outright and runs within 12% in another four; time ratios (Fonts over HarfBuzzSharp) Devanagari 0.83x, Balinese 0.88x, Hebrew 0.98x, Myanmar Zawgyi 0.95x, Thai 1.09x, Myanmar 1.10x, Khmer 1.12x (three scripts not quoted).
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet 'Gate' job: 3 launches, 5 warmup and 15 iterations on the host .NET 10 runtime (read from tests/SixLabors.Fonts.Benchmarks/SixLabors.Fonts.Benchmarks/Config.cs); no extra compiler flags
stars_or_usage: 350 stars; managed text layout engine for the SixLabors.ImageSharp.Drawing stack
tradeoffs: Pure managed .NET shaper with no native dependency, so it ships to any .NET 8+ target; it covers GSUB/GPOS and complex scripts, but the glyph output is not guaranteed identical to HarfBuzz; the Six Labors Split License gives Apache-2.0 terms only to qualifying open-source use and requires a paid licence for other commercial use, so it is not an OSI licence (no SPDX id; license field left null).
caveats: Snippet only: sixlabors.com is blocked here, so the ratios come from a web-search result summary of the release post and were not seen on the page; the three remaining scripts (Latin, Arabic, Hangul) were not quoted and by the post's own wording trail HarfBuzz by more than 12%, so the honest claim is competitive, not faster overall; the quoted ratios list four values below 1.0 (Devanagari, Balinese, Zawgyi, Hebrew) while the summary says three outright wins, so the snippet is internally inconsistent. The benchmark code is public (ShapeTextBenchmark.cs sets HarfBuzz via HarfBuzzSharp as the BenchmarkDotNet baseline, shaping one short run per script) but the repo does not carry result files, CPU model or OS, so tier A is not met.
found_via: WebSearch 'C# .NET font rendering library benchmark faster than FreeType SkiaSharp SixLabors.Fonts', then a second search for the 3.1.0 figures; benchmark code opened at github.com/SixLabors/Fonts/tree/main/tests/SixLabors.Fonts.Benchmarks

name: text-shaper
baseline: harfbuzzjs (HarfBuzz compiled to WebAssembly, driven from JavaScript); opentype.js also compared
workload: OpenType shaping of word, sentence and paragraph texts in Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar and CJK with Noto fonts, plus glyph path extraction and text to SVG, run under Bun with a batch timer (bench/shaping.test.ts).
claimed_speedup: README table, text-shaper vs harfbuzzjs: path extraction 16x faster, text to SVG 1.2-1.5x, Latin shaping 1.5x, Arabic 1.2x, Hebrew 1.6x, Hindi 3.6x, Myanmar 10.5x, CJK 1.3-1.5x. Versus opentype.js: 4x to 86x faster.
tradeoffs: Pure TypeScript (zero dependencies, runs in browsers and Bun/Node), so not usable from C++. Also does TrueType hinting and FreeType-style or libass-style rasterization. Young project (npm 0.1.x).
caveats: The baseline is the WebAssembly build of HarfBuzz called through the harfbuzzjs API, and each timed call creates a buffer, adds text, shapes and reads the result, so JavaScript-to-WASM boundary overhead is part of what is measured; this is not a comparison with native HarfBuzz, which is faster than both in practice. No hardware, Bun version or runtime flags are stated. Only 3 timed iterations per benchmark in the harness. Test fonts and texts come from a reference/rustybuzz/benches path that is not in the repo tree I opened.
found_via: Linked as 'text-shaper (a HarfBuzz alternative)' from the diffusionstudio/slug-webgpu README, found by WebSearch 'Slug library GPU glyph rendering directly from outlines'; README and bench/shaping.test.ts read via npm registry metadata, github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: TiTanF
baseline: RustType and ab_glyph (widely used pure-Rust glyph rasterizers); Fontdue also measured; FreeType is not included
workload: Rasterizing an 84-character string of mixed CJK and Latin characters with NotoSansSC-Medium at 10px, 200px and 320px.
claimed_speedup: README table: 10px 71.0 us (TiTanF) vs 245.6 us (RustType) and 222.6 us (ab_glyph); 200px 1.45 ms vs 3.21 ms and 3.07 ms; 320px 3.13 ms vs 7.27 ms and 6.77 ms; Fontdue is faster at 10px (54.3 us) but slower at 200px (1.60 ms) and 320px (4.02 ms).
tradeoffs: Dependency-free no_std Rust TrueType rasterizer; scales better than Fontdue for large glyphs and loses to it for small sizes; TrueType outlines only as far as the README states, with no shaping or hinting.
caveats: Own-repo benchmark with no compiler flags, CPU or run count in the README, and only one font and string; baselines are other Rust rasterizers, not FreeType, so the claim does not transfer to the stated FreeType baseline. Tiny, new project (3 stars).
found_via: WebSearch 'font rasterizer "times faster than FreeType" glyph rendering github', then github.com/Hoteira/titanf README and /commits

name: ttf-parser
baseline: FreeType (FT_Load_Glyph with FT_LOAD_NO_SCALE, glyph outlining); stb_truetype also compared
workload: Time to outline every glyph of a font (callbacks that only count move/line/quad/cubic segments) for glyf, glyf with gvar variations, CFF and CFF2 fonts; benchmark is C++ (benches/outline/outline.cc, Google Benchmark) calling FreeType, stb_truetype and the ttf-parser C API.
claimed_speedup: x86 (AMD 3700X), ms to outline all glyphs, ttf-parser vs FreeType: glyf 0.901 vs 1.171, gvar 2.972 vs 4.132, CFF 1.197 vs 5.647, CFF2 1.968 vs 6.392. ARM (Apple M1): glyf 0.550 vs 0.854, gvar 2.270 vs 4.594, CFF 1.054 vs 5.223, CFF2 1.765 vs 5.995. Derived from page data: x86 1.30x, 1.39x, 4.72x, 3.25x; M1 1.55x, 2.02x, 4.96x, 3.40x. On plain glyf, stb_truetype is faster than ttf-parser on x86 (0.675 ms) but slower on M1 (0.703 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Release builds per benches/outline/README.md (cargo build --release for the C API, meson --buildtype release); compiler names and versions not stated; FreeType is the system freetype2 library (>=2.8) and its version is not stated
hardware: AMD 3700X (x86) and Apple M1 (ARM)
tradeoffs: Parser and outliner only: no rasterization, no shaping, no hinting. Safe Rust, zero allocation, zero dependencies; C API is basic. The repo is in maintenance mode (bug fixes only, no new features or performance work) and recommends fontations (read-fonts and skrifa) for new projects.
caveats: The performance table is no longer in the current README; it is in tagged releases (read from v0.25.1, same table in v0.20.0). The author's own note under the table: 'FreeType is surprisingly slow, so I'm worried that I've messed something up.' FreeType is only asked for unscaled outlines, which is a narrow task (not rasterization). Benchmark code is public and CPUs are named, but compiler and flags are only 'release', so this sits just under tier A. Wins on plain glyf are modest (1.3x to 1.55x).
found_via: WebSearch 'font subsetting OR font parsing C OR C++ library "faster than" fonttools OR FreeType benchmark github' surfaced the crate; then read the current README, CONTRIBUTING.md, benches/outline/{README.md,meson.build,outline.cc} and the v0.20.0 README raw file
WebSearch (paper sites blocked): 'ttf-parser faster than FreeType benchmark glyph outline'; table read from the v0.25.1 README via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Typr.js
baseline: opentype.js (the widely used JavaScript OpenType font parser; HarfBuzz and FreeType are not measured)
workload: Parsing TTF/OTF/TTC/WOFF font files into a JavaScript font object, compared with opentype.js; the README gives no corpus, machine or timing table.
claimed_speedup: README: 'ultra fast (2x to 5x faster parsing than opentype.js)'
stars_or_usage: about 1k stars; main text engine of the Photopea image editor
tradeoffs: Static-function API over plain JavaScript objects with no classes; shaping (Typr.U.shape) covers ligatures, kerning and variable-font axes but is much less complete than HarfBuzz; 110 kB unminified, 4x smaller than opentype.js.
caveats: First-party one-line claim with no benchmark code, corpus, machine, browser or timing numbers in the repo, so it cannot be reproduced from the README; the baseline is opentype.js, not HarfBuzz or FreeType, and parsing speed does not measure shaping or rasterization. Recent commits are mostly 'Add files via upload' and README edits.
found_via: WebSearch 'Typr.js font parser faster than opentype.js benchmark', then github.com/photopea/Typr.js README and /commits

name: ucstrcase
baseline: icu::UnicodeString::caseCompare (ICU4C); strcasecmp also timed
workload: Case-insensitive comparison of generated UTF-8 strings, generated ASCII strings and worst-case matching UTF-8 strings (README timing loop; sizes and iteration counts not stated).
claimed_speedup: README: '5x-10x faster than icu::UnicodeString::caseCompare'. Timings: generated UTF-8 225 ms vs 3604 ms for ICU (strcasecmp 368 ms); generated ASCII 194 ms vs 4486 ms (strcasecmp 360 ms); worst-case matching UTF-8 3069 ms vs 12730 ms (strcasecmp 1988 ms). Ratios (derived from page data): about 16x, 23x and 4.1x faster than ICU.
tradeoffs: C library (usable from C++; vcpkg port files are in the ports directory) for caseless UTF-8 comparison using perfect hashing, adapted from Charlie Vieth's strcase (Go). Handles Unicode simple case folding only as implemented by its tables; not a full-collation or normalization-aware comparison. Worst case is about 50% slower than strcasecmp, which ignores non-ASCII.
caveats: README gives timings with no hardware, compiler, flags, workload sizes, ICU version or benchmark source link, so numbers are unverifiable first-party figures. The text's '5x-10x' headline is inconsistent with its own table (ratios from 4.1x to 23x). Only 8 commits, all on one day in July 2024. Category fit is poor: case-insensitive string comparison, not shaping, rasterization or layout; probably belongs with string or Unicode utilities.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ Unicode library case folding normalization "faster than ICU" "utf8proc" benchmark github'; README fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com and repo and commits pages opened.

name: ugrapheme
baseline: PyICU (ICU character BreakIterator); also pyuegc, uniseg and grapheme, the other Python grapheme splitters
workload: Splitting the string 'Hello 👩🏽‍🔬! 👩🏼‍❤️‍💋‍👨🏾 अनुच्छेद' into extended grapheme clusters (UAX #29) in IPython %%timeit.
claimed_speedup: README: ugrapheme grapheme_split 337 ns vs PyICU 2.84 us (about 8x); pyuegc 8.19 us (24x); uniseg 14.6 us (45x, also splits Devanagari conjuncts incorrectly); grapheme 17.4 us (52x, also incorrect).
tradeoffs: Cython extension with sparse bitmap property tables (under 11 KB) and a small DFA; passes the Unicode 16.0 UAX #29 grapheme break tests; behaves like a Python str with grapheme indexing; needs a compiled wheel.
caveats: Single short string, interactive %%timeit, no hardware, CPU or Python version stated; the PyICU run pays UnicodeString conversion cost per call (the README notes this itself), so the 8x ICU gap is partly binding overhead. Last commit 2024-10-28.
found_via: Fetched raw README after browsing github.com/topics/grapheme-clusters

name: uni-algo
baseline: ICU (word break and extended grapheme cluster break iteration over UTF-16 text)
workload: Unicode text segmentation (UAX #29 word breaks and extended grapheme cluster breaks) over a 'real text' sample in UTF-16, five consecutive runs per configuration.
claimed_speedup: MSVC 19.12 x64, first run: word breaks 2355.47 (uni-algo) vs 11379.4 (ICU), ~4.8x; grapheme breaks 2067.16 vs 5600.95, ~2.7x. MSVC 19.12 x86: word breaks 2544.55 vs 13137.1, ~5.2x; grapheme breaks 2239.48 vs 6766.44, ~3.0x (ratios derived from page data; units are not stated, lower is assumed better).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.12 (Visual Studio 2017 15.5.5), x64 and x86, flags not stated; GCC 7.3 -O3 rows exist but the ICU column is 0 there (ICU not built under MinGW)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 library with optional compiled Unicode data, UTF-8/16/32 support and safe iterators with bounds checks in debug. The README lists the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm and the Line Breaking Algorithm as planned for future versions, so it does not yet cover bidi or line breaking, only word and grapheme segmentation (plus case, normalization and collation). Dual licensed Public Domain or MIT.
caveats: Category fit is weak: the benchmarked task is Unicode segmentation, a pre-step of text layout, not font shaping or rasterization, and the baseline is ICU rather than HarfBuzz or FreeType. Results use 2018-era toolchains (GCC 7.3, MSVC 2017), and the perf commits date from April 2023. The result file states no units, no CPU model, no ICU version and no description of the text sample; ICU was measured only under MSVC. The author calls his own perf test 'a mess', and the README claims only performance 'at least the same as other implementations'. Only the UTF-16 segmentation test exists because ICU cluster breaks do not support UTF-8.
found_via: WebSearch 'bidi line break grapheme library C benchmark faster than ICU FriBidi github' surfaced the repo; then read README (Performance section), perf/main.cpp and perf/result/segment_utf16.md

name: uniwidth
baseline: mattn/go-runewidth (the common Go terminal display-width library) and rivo/uniseg; ICU, HarfBuzz and FreeType are not involved
workload: StringWidth and RuneWidth on ASCII, CJK, mixed, emoji, flag, ZWJ and real-world TUI strings in a separate bench/ module.
claimed_speedup: bench/README on Intel Core i7-1255U (Windows, amd64): ASCII short 9 ns vs 107 ns (go-runewidth) and 165 ns (uniseg); ASCII long (228 chars) 340 ns vs 5,380 ns and 8,058 ns; CJK short 96 ns vs 347 ns and 379 ns; mixed short 173 ns vs 469 ns and 632 ns; emoji short 158 ns vs 380 ns and 534 ns; ZWJ strings about 1x vs go-runewidth (323 ns vs 326 ns); top-level README headline '3-46x faster than go-runewidth'.
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5 -run=^$ in bench/ (library requires Go 1.25+; exact toolchain version not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i7-1255U, Windows, amd64
tradeoffs: Four-tier lookup tables plus 8-byte SWAR ASCII fast path with zero dependencies; allocates one []rune for medium and long non-ASCII strings; width of ZWJ and variation-selector sequences can differ from uniseg, which does full UAX #29 segmentation.
caveats: Own benchmark module with public code and a named CPU, but the Go toolchain version is not stated and results come from one Windows laptop; the top-level headline (3-46x, ASCII 15-46x) is larger than the measured table in bench/README (ASCII 12-24x, non-ASCII 2.4-4x, ZWJ about 1x), so quote the table. Baselines are Go libraries, not C++ HarfBuzz or FreeType, and display width is a text-layout primitive.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/wcwidth, then raw README and bench/README

name: uwcwidth
baseline: wcwidth (jquast/wcwidth, the standard Python terminal width library); cwcwidth also measured
workload: wcswidth of the string 'コンニチハ, セカイ!' in IPython %%timeit.
claimed_speedup: README: uwcwidth 41 ns vs wcwidth 1.73 us (about 40x) and cwcwidth 211 ns (about 5x); heading 'Performance: 40x faster than wcwidth'.
tradeoffs: Cython wrapper over about 4 KB of bitmap lookup tables derived from musl libc; covers Unicode 16.0 emoji with VS15/VS16 and ZWJ; width only, no grapheme segmentation (use ugrapheme for that).
caveats: One short string, no hardware, CPU or Python version; first-party numbers; the baseline is a pure-Python library, not HarfBuzz or FreeType, and terminal cell width is a text-layout primitive rather than shaping.
found_via: Fetched raw README while checking the ugrapheme author's companion library

name: uWrap
baseline: canvas-hypertxt (JavaScript canvas text-wrapping library)
workload: Wrapping 100,000 random sentences into boxes of random widths between 50px and 250px using Canvas2D measureText; run from the demo page's DevTools console.
claimed_speedup: README headline '10x faster'. Table: Chrome 135 82ms vs 770ms (about 9.4x, derived from page data); Firefox 137 90ms vs 1660ms (about 18x, derived from page data); Safari 18.1 185ms vs 1430ms (about 7.7x, derived from page data). README also says it is better in memory use and more accurate.
tradeoffs: Under 2KB minified. Only the pre-line wrapping strategy is implemented; works most accurately for Latin text; does not handle Windows-style \r\n line breaks. It predicts row heights for virtualized lists and does not do shaping.
caveats: Baseline is a third-party canvas wrapping helper, not HarfBuzz or FreeType, and not a widely recognised incumbent; this is text wrapping, at the edge of the shaping and layout category. Browser versions are named but the machine is not. The README says the baseline is less accurate, so the two do not compute identical output. Memory claim has no numbers.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN text layout engine paragraph line breaking bidi shaping fast written from scratch' surfaced the thread 'Show HN: uWrap.js' (item 43583478); repo README then opened.

name: xxUTF
baseline: ICU4C (unorm2 NFD normalization on UTF-8 input; also compared for NFC, NFKD, NFKC and case folding per README)
workload: NFD normalization of UTF-8 text in eight scripts (Arabic, Japanese, Chinese, Hindi, Russian, Latin, Hebrew, Korean; real text inputs under benchmarks/inputs), throughput in GB/s on an ARM NEON machine.
claimed_speedup: README states 'the fastest open source implementations of the supported algorithms' and shows only a bar chart (doc/neon_utf8_nfd.png). Approximate values read off that chart (not stated as numbers in the text): Arabic about 1.9 vs 0.5 GB/s, Japanese about 2.7 vs 0.8, Chinese about 4.1 vs 1.0, Hindi about 2.6 vs 0.7, Russian about 2.4 vs 0.5, Hebrew about 2.3 vs 0.6, Korean about 0.8 vs 0.25, Latin about 35 vs 0.35 GB/s (xxUTF vs ICU4C).
compiler_and_flags: Built with Zig 0.16.0, 'zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast' (README); benchmark runner is 'zig build bench'. ICU4C version and its build flags not stated.
hardware: Unnamed 'machine supporting ARM NEON'; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: C library distributed as a single-header amalgamation (callable from C++), no allocation, no libc dependency, UTF-8/UTF-16LE/UTF-16BE, NFD/NFC/NFKD/NFKC plus case folding, streaming helpers. Built for Unicode 17.0.0. README shows ARM NEON results and says not many instruction sets are supported yet (it claims to be fastest even in scalar mode). Build system is Zig 0.16.0. Input is assumed valid.
caveats: README publishes no numeric table, only a PNG chart for NFD on UTF-8 with NEON, so the numbers above are eyeballed from the image and approximate. The Latin bar (about 35 GB/s vs 0.35) is dominated by an already-normalized fast path and is not representative of text that needs decomposition. CPU model, compiler flags for ICU and ICU version are missing, which is why the tier is C and not A. The project calls itself alpha, with a security review still pending. Category fit is marginal (Unicode normalization and case folding, not shaping or rasterization); the baseline is ICU, not HarfBuzz or FreeType.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ Unicode library case folding normalization "faster than ICU" "utf8proc" benchmark github'; README fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com, chart doc/neon_utf8_nfd.png downloaded and viewed, commits page opened.

name: libgrapheme
baseline: ICU, GNU libunistring and libutf8proc (UAX #29 grapheme, word and sentence segmentation, UAX #14 line break detection, case conversion, UTF-8 decode)
workload: Unicode text segmentation (grapheme clusters, words, sentences, line break opportunities) and case conversion on UTF-8 strings and codepoint arrays; the repo's benchmark/ directory times libgrapheme against libutf8proc on the Unicode conformance test strings.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'It is also way smaller and much faster than the other established Unicode string libraries (ICU, GNU's libunistring, libutf8proc).'
compiler_and_flags: Repo default config.mk: CC=cc, CFLAGS=-std=c99 -Os -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic; benchmark binaries link -lutf8proc; no published benchmark run
stars_or_usage: 15 stars on the author's GitHub copy; canonical repo is git.suckless.org/libgrapheme (blocked here); suckless library
tradeoffs: Freestanding C99 library, no libc needed at runtime, heavily compressed lookup tables generated from Unicode 17.0.0 data, about 400 KB per the suckless page snippet. Scope is segmentation, case mapping and bidi only: no normalization, no shaping, no collation, no locale handling (ICU covers all of those).
caveats: Tier D slot: claim is qualitative. The repo ships benchmark programs (benchmark/character.c compares grapheme_next_character_break against utf8proc_grapheme_break_stateful, and util.c prints the ratio) but no results, hardware or flags are published in the files I opened, and no ICU or libunistring benchmark exists in the repo. The suckless project page, where results may be listed, and git.suckless.org are blocked here. README conformance section still says Unicode 15.0.0 while the intro says 17.0.0. A verifier with a C toolchain can run make benchmark (needs libutf8proc) to turn this into tier A for the utf8proc comparison.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'libgrapheme benchmark faster than ICU libunistring grapheme cluster' (result snippet from libs.suckless.org/libgrapheme, page blocked); README and benchmark/ sources opened via github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Pathfinder 3
baseline: FreeType CPU rasterizer (inferred: the README says only 'the best CPU rasterizers')
workload: GPU (OpenGL, Metal, WebGL) rasterization of font glyphs and vector paths with exact-coverage anti-aliasing, tiled and compute-based.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Even on lower-end GPUs, Pathfinder often matches or exceeds the performance of the best CPU rasterizers. The difference is particularly pronounced at large sizes, where Pathfinder regularly achieves multi-factor speedups.' No numbers.
tradeoffs: Needs a GPU and OpenGL 3.0+/ES 3.0+/WebGL 2/Metal; not a drop-in FreeType replacement (no hinting beyond slight hinting, no shaping). Callable from C or C++ through the C bindings, which the README calls less complete than the Rust API. README says it is under heavy development and incomplete.
caveats: Qualitative claim with no named baseline and no numbers in the repo; FreeType as the baseline is my inference from the font-rasterizer category and from a search-result summary mentioning a dated FreeType comparison chart in the 2017 Pathfinder blog post, which I could not open. Treat as tier D, include only as a lead. Other search results say the project is no longer under active development even though commits continue.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN fast 2D vector graphics renderer' and 'Show HN 2D vector graphics library Zig OR Rust OR Go anti-aliased rasterizer faster than Cairo' surfaced the thread 'Pathfinder, a fast GPU-based font rasterizer in Rust' and several comments naming Pathfinder as the best free-software GPU path renderer; repo README opened on github.com (also via raw.githubusercontent.com).

WebSearch (paper sites blocked): 'font rendering glyph rasterization text layout paper faster than FreeType' and 'Pathfinder GPU font rasterizer Patrick Walton benchmark compared to FreeType'; README and commits page read on github.com

name: Pretext
baseline: Browser DOM text measurement (getBoundingClientRect, offsetHeight and the layout reflow they trigger)
workload: Measuring multiline text height and line breaks in the browser without DOM layout: prepare() once per text, then layout() as pure arithmetic over cached widths.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in the project README, which says 'Fast, accurate' and that it side-steps getBoundingClientRect/offsetHeight reflow, 'one of the most expensive operations in the browser'. Third-party list descriptions on the GitHub text-layout topic page call it '500x faster than browser layout' (bluedusk/awesome-pretext) and expo-pretext lists '~0.0002ms JS layout'; these are not measurements in the repo.
tradeoffs: Layout only: the browser still paints the text, and it reads font widths through canvas measureText, so correctness depends on the host font engine; no bidi levels or visual order; not a general CSS inline formatting engine; in a worker small emoji measure too wide in Chrome and Firefox on macOS. JavaScript, not usable from C++.
caveats: Tier D: the repo documents a harness and many internal before/after benchmarks (RESEARCH.md, bun harness bench) but no head-to-head DOM versus Pretext table was found in README, RESEARCH.md, DEVELOPMENT.md or thoughts.md; the 500x figure is a third-party tagline. Included as the one notable (50k stars) tier D entry; the verifier should look in pages/ or the harness for an actual DOM comparison. Baseline is not HarfBuzz or FreeType, and the work is text measurement and line breaking, not glyph shaping.
found_via: WebFetch github.com/topics/text-layout (pretext ecosystem repos expo-pretext and awesome-pretext); README, RESEARCH.md, DEVELOPMENT.md, thoughts.md read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: fpng
baseline: libpng
workload: Lossless 24/32bpp PNG encode, and decode of fpng-produced PNGs, single-threaded, on the QOI benchmark suite (QOIR harness) and on 303 GPU-texture test images (fpng README).
claimed_speedup: README text: about 23x faster compression and 2.5-3x faster decompression than libpng (decompression only on fpng-compressed PNGs). QOIR benchmark: fpng encode 192.16 MPixels/s vs libpng 5.49 (about 35x, derived from page data) and decode 148.19 vs 56.18 (about 2.6x, derived from page data); output files about 1.29x larger than libpng (CmpRatio 0.3115 vs 0.2423, derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.1 (Debian Bullseye); QOIR script/run_full_benchmarks.sh builds the adapters with -Wall -O3 -march=native; the libpng and libwebp under test are the Debian Bullseye system builds; fpng's own README: MSVC 2019, gcc/clang need -msse4.1 -mpclmul -fno-strict-aliasing
hardware: Intel Core i5-10210U @ 1.60GHz (author's desktop machine), single-threaded; fpng README: Xeon E5-2690 3.00 GHz
tradeoffs: Encoder writes standards-conformant PNG readable by any decoder, but the fast decoder only accepts PNGs written by fpng (returns FPNG_DECODE_NOT_FPNG otherwise). 24/32bpp only. SIMD (SSE4.1 plus PCLMUL for CRC and Adler) is x86 only. Output about 29% larger than libpng. Single source file, no dependencies. README recommends Wuffs for decoding untrusted PNGs.
caveats: fpng's own README table has no libpng row, so the libpng ratios are a text claim there; the libpng numbers above come from the QOIR author's harness, which uses Debian's libpng at its default level. Decoder speed advantage applies only to fpng-encoded files; README says Wuffs is within about 10% on those.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'fast lossless image codec faster than libpng PNG encoder decoder github fpng fpnge benchmark' surfaced the codec; numbers from the QOIR benchmark page
WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' (result richgel999/fpng); opened README and cross-checked against nigeltao/qoir doc/full_benchmarks.txt

name: fpnge
baseline: libpng
workload: Lossless PNG encode speed (encoder only) on the QOI benchmark suite in the QOIR harness; fpnge README quotes 180 to 800 MP/s per core on a Threadripper 3970x.
claimed_speedup: QOIR benchmark: PNG/fpnge encode 312.59 MPixels/s vs PNG/libpng 5.49 (about 57x, derived from page data) at CmpRatio 0.2798 vs libpng 0.2423 (about 15% larger files, derived). fpnge README: speed on a single core is anywhere from 180 to 800 MP/s on a Threadripper 3970x (no libpng comparison on that page).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.1 (Debian Bullseye); QOIR script/run_full_benchmarks.sh builds the adapters with -Wall -O3 -march=native; the libpng and libwebp under test are the Debian Bullseye system builds
hardware: Intel Core i5-10210U @ 1.60GHz (author's desktop machine), single-threaded; fpnge README: Threadripper 3970x
tradeoffs: Encoder only, no decoder. AVX2 (x86 only); QOIR notes no ARM SIMD. Supports 8 and 16 bit content, 1 to 4 channels, optional cICP chunk for HDR. Uses a fixed special Huffman table so files are larger than libpng's.
caveats: Described by its author as a proof-of-concept demo; the fpnge repo itself carries no comparison against libpng, so the ratio comes from the QOIR author's harness with Debian's libpng at default settings.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'fast lossless image codec faster than libpng PNG encoder decoder github fpng fpnge benchmark' surfaced the codec; numbers from the QOIR benchmark page

WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' and 'github PNG encoder decoder library C++ faster than libpng ...' (fpnge listed); opened README and nigeltao/qoir benchmarks

name: image-png (Rust png crate)
baseline: libpng 1.6.37 (Debian Bullseye)
workload: PNG decode speed in the Wuffs 'mimic' benchmarks on six test images (19k 8bpp to 4002k 24bpp), Rust 1.48 with png 0.17.5, deflate 1.0.0, miniz_oxide 0.5.3 vs libpng 1.6.37.
claimed_speedup: Wuffs benchmarks.md: rust_png decode 187 vs libpng 122 MB/s (1.53x), 260 vs 147 (1.77x), 330 vs 370 (0.89x), 299 vs 289 (1.03x), 264 vs 214 (1.23x). Crate README: 'Performance is typically on par with or better than libpng' and an fdeflate-powered fast encoding mode 'dramatically faster than the fastest mode of libpng while simultaneously providing better compression ratio' (no numbers on that page).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.48 `cargo run --release` (script/bench-rust-png), png 0.17.5; libpng built with gcc 10.2.1 on Debian Bullseye
hardware: Intel Core i5-10210U @ 1.60GHz
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no unsafe code, fuzzed on OSS-Fuzz, so it is not callable from C++ without bindings. Also supports APNG. Fast encode mode uses fdeflate (already catalogued separately).
caveats: Mixed result: one of five images is slower than libpng (0.89x). The only numbers are for png 0.17.5 from 2022; current versions are not re-measured here. The fast-encode claim has no numbers on the crate page. zune-image's own criterion table (Apple platform, Rust) shows image-rs/png faster than the spng binding on all four PNG decode cases listed (for example 149.3 ms vs 297.4 ms on a baseline image).
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'JPEG decoder faster than libjpeg-turbo SIMD GPU paper github' and 'fast lossless image codec ...' led to the Wuffs benchmarks page; crate README opened

name: jpeg-nitro (nitrojpeg and nitropng parallel decoders)
baseline: libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 (AVX2, single thread) for JPEG; Wuffs for PNG
workload: Decode-only time per image from memory, one image decoded on all cores: 50 camera JPEGs (mostly 6000x4000, 17 MB average) and 34 real PNGs (938 MB, 805 Mpixel).
claimed_speedup: JPEG on the Intel i9 with 16 threads: nitrojpeg 11.7 ms per image versus libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 (AVX2) 124 ms to BGRX and 107 ms to YUV planes, about 9x to 11x (derived from page data). Single-threaded nitrojpeg 103 ms versus libjpeg-turbo 107 ms, about parity. On a Core i7-1260P (Linux) 5.4 ms parallel versus 32.3 ms on one thread. PNG on the i9: nitropng parallel 45.5 ms versus Wuffs 180 ms, about 4x (derived); libpng is not in the PNG table.
compiler_and_flags: clang -O3 -march=native -fblocks (README build commands; the Makefile also adds -mbranches-within-32B-boundaries on x86); libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 is built by scripts/get-deps.sh with flags not stated
hardware: Intel i9 13th gen, 8 cores / 16 threads, macOS (exact SKU not stated); also Apple M1, Xeon E3-1245 v5 and Core i7-1260P (Arch Linux)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; 82 commits, earliest visible commits dated 2026-09-27
tradeoffs: Baseline sequential JPEG only (progressive JPEG is left to libjpeg-turbo or the OS decoder); 8-bit non-interlaced PNG only; plain C with pthreads and AVX2 or NEON, but the loop bodies are clang blocks so it needs clang with -fblocks (GCC is not supported); uses every core for a single image, which helps latency but not total throughput of a batch; output is claimed bit-identical to libjpeg-turbo (checked by the author's bench/verify).
caveats: The headline 9x to 11x compares all-core decoding with libjpeg-turbo on one thread; at one thread nitrojpeg is only on par with libjpeg-turbo. Very new repository with no stars and a single author's benchmark. The i9 SKU is not named (the i7-1260P run is a different image set). The PNG baseline is Wuffs, not libpng. libjpeg-turbo gets no restart-marker parallelism because camera JPEGs lack restart markers.
found_via: WebSearch 'JPEG decoder encoder faster than libjpeg-turbo benchmark github'; opened the repo README and bench tables

name: libjxl fast_lossless (fjxl) encoder
baseline: libpng and libwebp (lossless encoders)
workload: Lossless encode of the QOI benchmark suite with libjxl's experimental fast_lossless encoder (regular libjxl decoder) in the QOIR harness, single-threaded, vs libpng and libwebp lossless; WangXuan95's CLIC2021 shootout with cjxl -e 1.
claimed_speedup: QOIR benchmark: JXL_Lossless/f encode 106.48 MPixels/s vs libpng 5.49 (about 19x, derived from page data) and libwebp lossless 2.49 (about 43x, derived), with smaller files than libpng (CmpRatio 0.2171 vs 0.2423, about 10% smaller, derived). Decode is slower: 33.16 MPixels/s vs libpng 56.18 and libwebp 89.94. WangXuan95 CLIC2021 shootout (cjxl v0.9.0 -q 100 -e 1): 42.993 s compress, 57.650 s decompress, 1,648,242,164 bytes vs Pillow PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 s, 33.677 s, 2,003,016,524 bytes (derived: 7.8x faster encode, 18% smaller, 1.7x slower decode).
compiler_and_flags: QOIR adapter built with -march=native -DFASTLL_ENABLE_AVX2_INTRINSICS=1 plus -Wall -O3 under gcc 10.2.1; libpng and libwebp are Debian Bullseye system builds
hardware: Intel Core i5-10210U @ 1.60GHz (author's desktop machine), single-threaded
tradeoffs: The fast-lossless mode trades ratio for speed (libjxl effort 7 compresses to CmpRatio 0.1548 but encodes at 0.57 MPixels/s). Needs JPEG XL support on the consumer side. The fast encoder uses AVX2 intrinsics. Single-threaded decode is slower than libpng and libwebp in that table.
caveats: Numbers date from the 2022 experimental/fast_lossless build in the QOIR harness; later libjxl versions may differ and were not re-measured. Encode-only win: decode is slower than both baselines. Measured by the author of a different codec (QOIR) and by a separate shootout (WangXuan95), both on laptop-class CPUs.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'fast lossless image codec faster than libpng PNG encoder decoder github fpng fpnge benchmark' surfaced the codec; numbers from the QOIR benchmark page
Named as 'JXL_Lossless/f' in nigeltao/qoir doc/full_benchmarks.txt; github.com/topics/jpeg?l=c%2B%2B listed libjxl; opened lib/jxl/enc_fast_lossless.h, commits page

name: libspng
baseline: libpng 1.6.37 (Debian Bullseye)
workload: PNG decode speed in the Wuffs project's 'mimic' benchmarks on six test images from 19k (8bpp) to 4002k (24bpp) decoded bytes, libspng 0.7.3 vs libpng 1.6.37.
claimed_speedup: Wuffs benchmarks.md: libspng decode 125 vs libpng 122 MB/s (1.02x), 155 vs 147 (1.05x), 384 vs 370 (1.04x), 392 vs 289 (1.36x, 552k 32bpp, verify checksum; 461 MB/s ignoring checksum, 1.60x vs libpng's verify-checksum baseline), 225 vs 214 (1.05x). libspng README: 'it outperforms the reference implementation in common use cases' (performance chart is an image on libspng.org, not opened). MANGO's README table (first-party rival) shows spng encode 215.9 ms vs libpng 820.5 ms on a 2560x1600 image.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.1 and clang 11.0.1 on Debian Bullseye; libpng 1.6.37 and libspng 0.7.3 run through Wuffs' `wuffs bench -mimic` harness (the doc shows the `gcc -O3 test/c/std/<codec>.c` pattern for reproducing std/ benchmarks)
hardware: Intel Core i5-10210U @ 1.60GHz
tradeoffs: Simpler API than libpng, not API-compatible; security focus (OSS-Fuzz); does not require zlib (optional miniz); encoder included; progressive read supported; animated PNG still planned. Same file format so output is interchangeable.
caveats: Decode gains are only 2 to 5% on four of the six images; the big wins are on the 32bpp image and depend on skipping checksums. Wuffs measured libspng 0.7.3 in September 2022; later versions are not re-measured. The Wuffs project is itself a competing PNG decoder.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'fast lossless image codec faster than libpng ...' surfaced the PNG library field; libspng README and the Wuffs doc/benchmarks.md page carry the numbers
WebSearch 'lossless image codec faster than libwebp lossless PNG encoder decoder C++ github benchmark' surfaced the Wuffs blog; its appendix lists libspng; confirmed with the libspng README

name: PNG XL (PXL)
baseline: libpng (decode into raw RGBA pixels)
workload: Decoding the 24 Kodak lossless photographs from in-memory compressed bytes straight to a raw pixel buffer, single thread, median of 15 repeats per file, summed over the 24 files (bench/rawdec); also size-versus-decode-speed charts on photographs and synthetic stills against libpng, QOI, WebP, JPEG XL and AVIF.
claimed_speedup: Raw-pixel decode over 24 Kodak photographs: libpng 333.6 ms total vs PXL 143.2 ms (README: 'PXL decodes ~2.3x faster than libpng and its files are 14.5% smaller'; QOI 120.7 ms is faster still but files are 103.5% of PNG). Photographs: PXL about twice libpng speed (libpng 98.6 MB/s vs PXL 200-276 MB/s) at 85.6% of source PNG size. Synthetic stills: PXL 485 MB/s vs libpng 309 MB/s, but WebP wins both axes there (570 MB/s, 44.6%). On a real PSP-3008 (333 MHz) three of four filters beat libpng by 2.8-3.5x while the adaptive filter only ties.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 16.1.1 / 16.2.1, CMake Release build (-O2, later -O3), no -march=native; libpng 1.6, zstd 1.5.7 (docs/BENCHMARKS.md).
hardware: Intel Pentium B960 @ 2.20GHz, 2 cores, 15.2 GiB RAM (docs/BENCHMARKS.md); also a real PSP-3008 at 333 MHz.
stars_or_usage: 7 stars; used by the repo's own Qt image plugin, Dolphin thumbnailer and FFmpeg module
tradeoffs: A new lossless format (.pxl, animated .apxl), not a PNG decoder: PNG row filters feeding Zstandard, with libpng used only to read and write real PNG files. Files are 85.5% of PNG on photographs but JPEG XL and WebP compress better; decoder is 174 KB .text versus libpng's 210 KB. Single-threaded decode; PNG files must be converted to PXL first.
caveats: Descends from Zpng (catid/Zpng, already catalogued). The comparison is format versus format: libpng decodes the original PNG while PXL decodes a .pxl file re-encoded from it (13.6 MB versus 15.9 MB total), so it is not two decoders on identical bytes. Benchmarked on a 2-core Pentium B960. README states libjxl and libavif were given no worker threads, QOI is about 16% faster than PXL on 24 of 24 files, and an earlier README chart overstated PXL by about a third before all outputs were forced to RGBA8. The author notes timing columns are not comparable across runs (the 2026-07-28 measurement was libpng 347.5 ms versus PXL 163.7 ms, 2.1x).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/lossless-image-compression listing led to LicaRedMoth/PNG-XL; opened README, docs/BENCHMARKS.md and commits page.

name: QLIC (Quick Lossless Image Codec)
baseline: libjxl lossless (JPEG XL effort 9) and libwebp lossless (preset 6); also OxiPNG level 6
workload: Lossless encode and decode of a 3,167-image corpus (1,964,362,720 pixels: DIV2K and CLIC 2022 validation, QOI benchmark categories, Enrico UI screenshots), one pinned logical processor, byte-exact roundtrip check on every file.
claimed_speedup: Encode: QLIC automatic policy 618.673 s vs JPEG XL lossless effort 9 5,674.173 s (about 9.2x faster, derived from page data) and vs OxiPNG level 6 9,105.634 s (about 14.7x, derived), with 1,160,913,984 bytes total vs 1,164,424,898 (JPEG XL e9) and 1,289,518,274 (WebP preset 6). Decode: QLIC 236.927 s (8.291 MP/s) vs JPEG XL effort 9 files 307.602 s (29.83% slower) while WebP preset 6 files decode in 117.887 s (16.663 MP/s), i.e. QLIC is about 2x slower than libwebp at decode and about 5% slower at encode than WebP preset 6 (585.964 s).
compiler_and_flags: QLIC portable x86-64 Clang 22.1.4 Release build, no -march=native, no PGO; baseline encoders are the stock JPEG XL and WebP tools (versions not stated on the page)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D, Windows 11, one pinned logical processor, encode order rotated
tradeoffs: Lossless only. Not the decode winner: libwebp decodes this corpus about twice as fast. Encode time is close to WebP preset 6, not faster. Ships C/C++ SDK, CLI, Windows GUI and WIC plugin, a Rust decoder and WebAssembly build; the Rust LZMS port keeps its MIT license. Very young project (first commit 2026-07-29, 1.0.0 on 2026-08-27).
caveats: Single-author benchmark of a project three months old; the speed win is measured against JPEG XL effort 9, an extreme setting; at JPEG XL effort 4 to 5 (497 s to 629 s) the encode time is similar and QLIC output is smaller by 4% to 6% (derived). Encode and decode wall times include process startup and file I/O. Baseline tool versions and exact baseline flags not stated on the page. Windows only measurements. Benchmark harness is public in the benchmark directory (PowerShell scripts, pinned corpus manifest with SHA-256), so the run is reproducible in principle.
found_via: Blogs / talks query: encode.su search 'fast lossless image codec github open source decode speed MB/s faster than PNG WebP JPEG XL' led to the lossless codec threads; QLIC found via GitHub topics page github.com/topics/image-codec and lossless-image-compression

name: QOI (Quite OK Image format)
baseline: libpng
workload: Lossless RGB/RGBA encode and decode of the QOI benchmark suite, single-threaded, in the QOIR harness (qoi.h reference implementation).
claimed_speedup: QOIR benchmark: QOI encode 146.87 MPixels/s vs libpng 5.49 (about 27x, derived from page data) and decode 193.53 vs 56.18 (about 3.4x, derived from page data); CmpRatio 0.2823 vs libpng 0.2423 (about 16% larger files, derived). The QOI README says throughput is a lot higher than libpng and points to qoiformat.org/benchmark (host blocked here, not opened).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.1 (Debian Bullseye); QOIR script/run_full_benchmarks.sh builds the adapters with -Wall -O3 -march=native; the libpng and libwebp under test are the Debian Bullseye system builds
hardware: Intel Core i5-10210U @ 1.60GHz (author's desktop machine), single-threaded
tradeoffs: Single-file C/C++ header library. Format is final and extremely simple but files are larger than libpng's (and much larger than WebP or JPEG XL). Not PNG-compatible. RGB and RGBA 8-bit only. Reference implementation is deliberately not heavily optimised and loads the whole file into RAM; limited to 400 million pixels.
caveats: Numbers are from a third-party harness (QOIR author), not from qoiformat.org, which I could not open. Compression is worse than libpng by about 16%, so this is a speed-for-size trade. Maintainers reject performance pull requests.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'fast lossless image codec faster than libpng PNG encoder decoder github fpng fpnge benchmark' surfaced the codec; numbers from the QOIR benchmark page
Referenced by the QOIR README and fpng README opened under WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com'; opened phoboslab/qoi README, Makefile and qoibench.c

name: qoi-asm (QOI codec in x86-64 assembly)
baseline: QOI reference C implementation (phoboslab/qoi qoi.h) compiled with gcc -O3 -march=x86-64-v3
workload: QOI encode and decode (3 and 4 channel) on 7 synthetic workloads: random RGBA and RGB, runs, photo-like, 16-colour palette, at 512x512 and 1080p; median of 11 or 31 reps, pinned core, bit-for-bit output check against the C oracle.
claimed_speedup: 1.07x to 2.16x faster than gcc -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 across all 18 benchmark rows, e.g. 1080p RGBA random encode 4.40 M vs 8.58 M TSC ticks (1.95x), 512x512 RGBA random decode to 4 channels 0.49 M vs 1.06 M (2.16x), 1080p RGBA photo-like decode 12.06 M vs 14.68 M (1.22x).
compiler_and_flags: Baseline: gcc -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 (and untouched oracle at -O2); gcc version not stated; assembly assembled with GNU as, Intel syntax
hardware: Intel Core i7-14700F (Raptor Lake, AVX2, no AVX-512), WSL2 Linux kernel 5.15, taskset -c 3
tradeoffs: Drop-in for qoi_encode, qoi_decode, qoi_write, qoi_read with the upstream ABI, but x86-64-v3 only (Haswell 2013 or newer; SIGILL on older CPUs, not portable to ARM). One assembly file in GNU as Intel syntax. Like upstream, qoi_decode may read a few bytes past the input on malformed streams.
caveats: Speedup is hand assembly (SSE4.1 delta computation, multiply hash) against the same algorithm compiled by gcc, so it measures compiler quality on one reference file, not a new algorithm. Workloads are synthetic (generated random, run, photo-like and palette images), one host, ratios in invariant-TSC ticks (README warns cycles understate core cycles by up to 2.4x; ns/op is also recorded). Repository has a single commit dated 2026-09-26; README says it was produced with a multi-agent AI workflow. 19,185 differential tests plus ASan and UBSan runs pass per README. Not compared against other QOI implementations such as qoixx or QOIR.
found_via: Blogs / talks query: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/image-codec sorted by recently updated (description 'faster than gcc -O3'), after WebSearch on image codec blog posts yielded mostly blocked pages

name: QOIR
baseline: libpng (Debian Bullseye build); also libwebp lossless
workload: Single-threaded lossless encode and decode of the QOI benchmark image suite (RGB and RGBA photos, screenshots, icons) in megapixels per second plus compression ratio, against libpng, libwebp, libjxl, fpng, fpnge, QOI, ZPNG, stb and Wuffs.
claimed_speedup: README: QOIR encodes 30x faster (0.033 vs 1.000) and decodes 4.9x faster (0.203 vs 1.000) than libpng. Raw table: QOIR_Lossless 168.90 MPixels/s encode and 276.45 decode vs PNG/libpng 5.49 and 56.18 and WebP_Lossless 2.49 and 89.94 (derived from page data: about 68x faster encode and 3.1x faster decode than libwebp lossless). Cost: CmpRatio 0.2525 vs libpng 0.2423 and libwebp 0.1651 (files about 4% larger than libpng, about 53% larger than lossless WebP, derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.1 (Debian Bullseye); QOIR script/run_full_benchmarks.sh builds the adapters with -Wall -O3 -march=native; the libpng and libwebp under test are the Debian Bullseye system builds
hardware: Intel Core i5-10210U @ 1.60GHz (author's desktop machine), single-threaded
tradeoffs: Not PNG: a new experimental container (README warns of incompatible changes), so consumers need QOIR support. 24-bit RGB and 32-bit RGBA only. Larger files than libpng and much larger than WebP or JPEG XL. Tiles allow multi-threaded decoding (README links a commit claiming over 3x faster). Ships its own LZ4; single-file C library with no dependencies; optional trivial lossy mode (8 to 6 bits per channel).
caveats: Author-run benchmark on one laptop-class CPU (about 9 hours for the full run); libpng and libwebp are Debian system binaries, not rebuilt with the same flags. AVIF was not measured (author could not get a lossless libavif encode working). The README itself notes ZPNG is sometimes strictly better. Format is experimental.

WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' (result nigeltao/qoir); opened README and doc/full_benchmarks.txt

name: Zpng
baseline: libpng
workload: Lossless photographic image compression (Zstd plus a simple colour transform and subtract filter) vs PNG; QOIR harness over the QOI benchmark suite and WangXuan95's CLIC2021 (585 RGB images) shootout.
claimed_speedup: QOIR benchmark: ZPNG_Lossless encode 126.21 MPixels/s and decode 256.32 vs libpng 5.49 and 56.18 (about 23x and 4.6x, derived from page data) with smaller output (CmpRatio 0.2182 vs 0.2423, about 10% smaller, derived). README: takes less than 6% of a PNG compressor's time and produces a file 66% of the size (one 13.9 MB photo). WangXuan95 CLIC2021 shootout: ZPNG 25.909 s compress and 24.083 s decompress, 1,755,786,378 bytes vs Pillow PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 s, 33.677 s, 2,003,016,524 bytes.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.1 (Debian Bullseye); QOIR script/run_full_benchmarks.sh builds the adapters with -Wall -O3 -march=native; the libpng and libwebp under test are the Debian Bullseye system builds; QOIR adapts ZPNG as lz4/zstd variants
hardware: Intel Core i5-10210U @ 1.60GHz (author's desktop machine), single-threaded; shootout: Intel Core i7 12700H, Windows 10
tradeoffs: Custom non-PNG format that needs Zstd (bundled in the repo). C API plus command-line tool, about 500 lines. Works best on photographic images. Author calls it experimental and does not expect others to use it.
caveats: No commits since 2018. README timing is one image on Windows with no compiler flags stated; the A tier rests on the QOIR harness, which uses an adapted copy of ZPNG. QOIR notes ZPNG is competitive with or better than QOIR on photographic subsets.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'fast lossless image codec faster than libpng PNG encoder decoder github fpng fpnge benchmark' surfaced the codec; numbers from the QOIR benchmark page
Named in nigeltao/qoir README (opened) from WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com'; opened Zpng README and the Image-Compression-Benchmark README

name: CharLS
baseline: Pillow PNG encoder and Pillow JPEG 2000 plugin (in Image-Compression-Benchmark); the README compares against the original HP JPEG-LS code, JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000
workload: Lossless compression and decompression of 585 CLIC2021 RGB 24-bit images (4.1 GB), single-threaded, total time and total size, using the CharLS-based pillow-jpls 1.3.2 plugin.
claimed_speedup: Image-Compression-Benchmark (CLIC2021, units not stated on page, presumably seconds): JPEG-LS compress 72.237 and decompress 66.567 vs JPEG2000 319.912 and 275.398 (about 4.4x and 4.1x faster, derived from page data) and vs PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 and 33.677 (4.6x faster compress but about 2x slower decompress); JPEG-LS total size 1931584595 vs JPEG2000 1992860964 and PNG 2003016524 bytes. CharLS README: 'about twice as fast as the original HP code, and beats both JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000 by a factor 3'.
compiler_and_flags: Python 3.9 with Pillow 10.1.0 and pillow-jpls 1.3.2 (CharLS wheel build flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i7 12700H, 16GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10
tradeoffs: JPEG-LS (ISO/IEC 14495-1) is a lossless/near-lossless codec with low complexity; decode is about twice as slow as Pillow's PNG decode in the cited suite. README notes Hewlett Packard patents on JPEG-LS (licensed free for conformant implementations; some may have expired). No SIMD: speed comes from templates and traits.
caveats: Weak fit to the listed baselines: none of libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp or libavif is directly compared, and Pillow's PNG codec uses zlib rather than libpng. The suite measures a Python wrapper (pillow-jpls, which PyPI says is based on CharLS), so Python overhead is included. The README's own 'twice as fast as HP code' claim cites a page on imagecompression.info that was not opened and is dated. Another JPEG-LS-family row ('JPEG-LS-ext') is a different codec and is not counted here.
found_via: github.com/topics/image-compression?l=c%2B%2B (team-charls/charls listed); opened README, LICENSE.md, commits page, the Image-Compression-Benchmark README and the pillow-jpls PyPI page

name: HALIC (High Availability Lossless Image Compression)
language: unknown (binaries only; README says built with GCC and Clang)
baseline: libwebp lossless (Pillow 10.1.0, method 1) and PNG (Pillow 10.1.0, optimize=False)
workload: Total compress and decompress time and compressed size on CLIC2021 (585 RGB images, 4.1 GB) and GDCC2020 (100 RGB images, 1.0 GB) in the Image-Compression-Benchmark shootout, all codecs single-threaded.
claimed_speedup: CLIC2021: HALIC 1,473,481,803 bytes, 22.187 s compress, 28.447 s decompress versus WebP lossless m1 1,496,478,650 bytes, 720.160 s, 37.044 s (about 32x faster compress, 1.3x faster decompress, 1.5% smaller, derived) and PNG optimize=False 2,003,016,524 bytes, 334.791 s, 33.677 s (about 15x compress, 1.18x decompress, 26% smaller, derived). GDCC2020: HALIC 4.780 s compress and 5.426 s decompress versus PNG optimize=False 152.321 s and 11.545 s (about 32x and 2.1x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated: most codecs are prebuilt Windows .exe files in the benchmark's codec folder, WebP and PNG run through Python 3.9 with Pillow 10.1.0; commands are listed in the README (PNG: Image.open('in.pnm').save('out.png', optimize=False))
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700H, 16 GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10; every codec single-threaded, SIMD allowed
tradeoffs: Binary releases only (Windows and Linux executables), PPM and PNM input, ANS (FSE) entropy coder with independent blocks, multithreading only from version 0.7 on. Compression ratio is behind JPEG XL, EMMA and NBLI; the 'HALIC fast' variant trades size for speed and failed to decompress one gray test image (zone_plate.pnm) in the benchmark.
caveats: The repository holds only README, LICENSE (MIT) and .gitignore; the benchmark's own format table marks HALIC as not open source, so the source cannot be inspected or rebuilt, and has_code is false even though the licence file says MIT. The numbers come from prebuilt executables with no flags. The PNG baseline is Pillow's zlib-based codec, not libpng. On tiny images PNG decodes faster (Kodak: PNG optimize=False 0.484 s versus HALIC 0.615 s), so the decode win shows only on large images. The author's own README charts carry no numbers.
found_via: Image-Compression-Benchmark README (WangXuan95/Image-Compression-Benchmark), found by WebSearch 'Image-Compression-Benchmark RunBenchmark.py github'

name: meshoptimizer (vertex codec used as a lossless float-image compressor)
baseline: OpenEXR ZIP compression (zlib), also compared with EXR PIZ, RLE, HTJ2K and libjxl lossless
workload: Lossless compression of 10 floating-point EXR images (3122 MB total, half and float, up to 37 channels), split into 16K-pixel chunks compressed in parallel; compression ratio versus GB/s, 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: The author's conclusion: 'mesh optimizer is very impressive ... very far ahead of others towards top right of the chart'. Approximate readings of the Ryzen 5950X chart: decompression about 8 GB/s versus about 2.4 GB/s for EXR ZIP (about 3.3x, derived) at compression ratios of about 1.9 to 2.03 versus 1.87 for ZIP; compression about 1.3 to 1.8 GB/s versus about 1.2 GB/s for ZIP. JPEG-XL and HTJ2K are slower; the README says EXR HTJ2K decompresses at 2x slower than ZIP.
compiler_and_flags: Release cmake builds: Visual Studio 2022 v17.14 on Windows, Xcode clang 16 on Mac; OpenEXR 3.4.0, libjxl pre-v0.12 (029cec4), meshoptimizer v0.25, zstd 1.5.7 fetched via FetchContent
hardware: Windows AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (16 threads); Mac MacBook Pro M4 Max
tradeoffs: Not an image format: the benchmark wraps meshoptimizer's vertex-data compression (vertex size set to the pixel size, padded to a multiple of four) in a custom chunked container written by the benchmark author, so there is no interoperability. Code size +26 KB (+431 KB with zstd) versus +308 KB for EXR HTJ2K and +6017 KB for JPEG-XL.
caveats: The figures are read off chart images, not text. Test images are mostly noisy path-traced renders and could behave differently on natural images, as the author notes. It is a test harness by Aras Pranckevicius, not a supported meshoptimizer image feature, and meshoptimizer's own purpose is mesh optimization, so it may be catalogued under other categories. Both sides are multithreaded.
found_via: Shootout sweep: aras-p/test_exr_htj2k_jxl, found via the 'OpenJPH vs OpenJPEG' WebSearch results

name: OpenJPH (HTJ2K encoder and decoder)
baseline: OpenJPEG (JPEG 2000 Part 1)
workload: Single-image decode time in the dicom-codecs shootout on three DICOM test images (8-bit color US, 12-bit gray MR, 16-bit gray CT); each codec decodes its own encoded stream, one iteration.
claimed_speedup: Decode: openjph 4.09 ms versus openjpeg 24.73 ms (8-bit color US), 1.43 ms versus 15.65 ms (12-bit gray MR), 1.53 ms versus 22.27 ms (16-bit gray CT), about 6x, 11x and 15x (derived from page data). Kakadu, which is proprietary, is faster still at 1.13, 0.51 and 0.64 ms.
hardware: Apple MacBook Pro M1 Pro
stars_or_usage: 296 stars; packaged in several distributions per the README's repology badge
tradeoffs: Implements High-Throughput JPEG 2000 (Part 15, ITU-T T.814) only, with Part 1 wavelet and coding features reused; it cannot read ordinary Part 1 JPEG 2000 files, so adoption needs HTJ2K-encoded data. The HT block coder trades some compression ratio for speed.
caveats: The two codecs decode different codestreams (HTJ2K for OpenJPH, JPEG 2000 Part 1 or HTJ2K for OpenJPEG depending on the test file, not stated), so part of the gap is the format rather than the library. One iteration per case, no compiler or flags, and the dicom-codecs repository calls itself WIP (10 stars). The OpenJPH README itself publishes no numbers and only links third-party papers (Kakadu ICIP 2019, blocked here).
found_via: WebSearch 'OpenJPH vs OpenJPEG vs Kakadu HTJ2K encode decode speed benchmark comparison' led to dicom-codecs/dicom-codecs

name: @napi-rs/image
baseline: sharp (Node.js binding over libvips with libwebp and libavif)
workload: One EXIF JPEG with orientation applied, resized to width 225 and encoded to WebP (quality 75) or AVIF (quality 70, 4:2:0), work submitted concurrently up to the CPU count.
claimed_speedup: Default thread pool: WebP 202 ops/s vs sharp 169 ops/s, AVIF 26 vs 24 ops/s. UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=10: WebP 431 vs 238 ops/s (README: 'The 1.8x ratio applies only to the recorded WebP pipeline with a thread pool of 10'), AVIF 36 vs 32 ops/s.
compiler_and_flags: node bench/bench.mjs (benchmark script in the repo); Node.js and package versions were not recorded with the results.
hardware: Apple M1 Max, macOS 12.3.1, arm64
tradeoffs: Rust native addon for Node.js (plus a WebAssembly build) that resizes, converts and optimizes JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF; HEIC not available in WASM. API differs from sharp. It is a Node.js packaging of native image codecs rather than a new codec design (README: Rust-powered image processing), so it may fold into the libwebp/libavif entries.
caveats: README labels the table 'historical results ... not a new benchmark of 1.15.0'; Node and package versions unrecorded; single input image; equal numeric quality settings do not guarantee equal visual quality or file size across encoders (README says so). The 1.8x win applies to one configuration; the other three configurations are 1.08x to 1.19x (derived from page data). Baseline is sharp, not libwebp or libavif directly.

name: Accelerating JPEG Decompression on GPUs (Weissenberger and Schmidt, HiPC 2021)
baseline: libjpeg-turbo (CPU) and NVIDIA nvJPEG (GPU)
workload: GPU JPEG decompression that locates codeword boundaries at arbitrary bitstream positions so independent chunks decode in parallel; compared on A100 and V100 GPUs against libjpeg-turbo and nvJPEG (also nvJPEG with the A100 hardware decoder).
claimed_speedup: From search-result snippet of the arXiv abstract (arXiv:2111.09219, paper page not opened): outperforms libjpeg-turbo (CPU) and nvJPEG (GPU) by up to 51x (34x) and 8.0x (5.7x) on A100 (V100), and up to 3.4x over nvJPEG with the dedicated hardware decoder on A100.
hardware: NVIDIA A100 and V100 GPUs (per snippet)
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA GPU and PCIe transfers; implements an important subset of the JPEG standard, not all of it. Presented at HiPC 2021 (peer reviewed). Related author repos on github.com/weissenberger (gpuhd, multians) cover GPU Huffman and ANS decoding, not a JPEG decoder.
caveats: Snippet only: arXiv, ACM and IEEE are blocked here, so the numbers are from search-result text and I could not read the paper or find its code (the author's GitHub profile lists gpuhd, multians, bzip2gpu and HIPSW4 but no JPEG decoder). Tier capped at C, has_code false.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'JPEG decoder faster than libjpeg-turbo SIMD GPU paper github' and '"Accelerating JPEG Decompression on GPUs" Weissenberger Schmidt github code'

Repository archived by the owner on 2026-01-28; the bc7enc_rdo README says bc7e.ispc was ported to plain C++ (basisu_bc7e_scalar.cpp in basis_universal) and that the newer bc7f is faster still.

name: bc7enc (rgbcx BC1 and bc7enc16 BC7 encoders)
baseline: libsquish (BC1 cluster fit); Intel ispc_texcomp (BC7); also AMD Compressonator and DirectXTex CPU BC7
workload: Encoding 31 images (Kodak corpus plus others) to BC1 and BC7, comparing total encode time and average PSNR at matched quality settings (multithreaded with OpenMP).
claimed_speedup: BC1 'prioritized cluster fit' is 3-4x faster than traditional cluster fit as in libsquish (SSE2) at the same or slightly higher average quality; rgbcx BC1 is faster than AMD Compressonator and libsquish at the same quality. BC7 perceptual (luma PSNR): ispc_texcomp slow 355.4 s 48.6 dB vs bc7enc16 38.3 s 49.6 dB (9.3x faster, derived from page data); ispc_texcomp fast 41.5 s 48.0 dB vs bc7enc16 20.8 s 49.3 dB (2.0x faster, derived from page data). BC7 non-perceptual: DirectXTex CPU default 9485.1 s 45.6 dB vs bc7enc16 36 s 46.0 dB (263x faster, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; multithreaded with OpenMP; ispc_texcomp called with 64 blocks at a time using AVX instructions
hardware: dual Xeon workstation (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: The BC7 encoder here supports only modes 1 and 6 for RGB (plus modes 5 and 7 for alpha) and is scalar, not vectorized, so it will not match full-mode encoders on every texture; the author points to bc7e and bc7enc_rdo for best BC7 quality. Single-source C/C++ with no dependencies; archived 2026-01-28.
caveats: The README says most timings are for the original release (the latest bc7enc16.c is 8-27% faster when mode 1 is enabled). The CPU model and compile flags are missing. In the non-perceptual ultrafast row ispc_texcomp is faster (1.9 s vs 3.8 s at 42.7 dB), so the win is not uniform. Dual-licensed: choose MIT or public domain (no patent grant for the public-domain option). DirectXTex run used a locally patched pbit bugfix.
found_via: WebSearch 'BC7 encoder fast SIMD faster than Compressonator OR ISPC Texture Compressor OR NVTT benchmark github C++' surfaced richgel999/bc7enc and BinomialLLC/bc7e; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Efficient Compression Tool (ECT)
baseline: zopfli (and gzip -9); the published benchmark is gzip/deflate on enwik8, not PNG
workload: Compressing enwik8 (100,000,000 bytes) into gzip format at ECT levels 1-9 versus gzip -9 and zopfli with 1, 5, 15 and 30 iterations.
claimed_speedup: ECT -3 35,014,543 bytes in 16.2 s vs zopfli -i15 34,966,078 bytes in 3m 59.9s (14.8x faster at 0.14% larger, derived from page data); ECT -2 35,019,440 bytes in 14.8 s vs zopfli -i5 34,983,757 bytes in 2m 12.0s (8.9x derived); ECT -9 34,937,781 bytes in 3m 17.9s vs zopfli -i30 34,961,453 bytes in 6m 30.6s (smaller and 2.0x faster, derived); ECT -1 36,493,257 bytes in 3.5 s vs gzip -9 36,475,811 bytes in 5.8 s.
compiler_and_flags: clang on macOS 12.5 (flags not stated); ECT v0.9.2
hardware: Intel i7-7700HQ

caveats: The README publishes no PNG or JPEG timings; the benchmark is deflate output on text, so this probably belongs under general lossless compression rather than image codecs. Mismatch flagged for the orchestrator. Single run table, old version (0.9.2).
found_via: Recalled as a known PNG/JPEG optimizer while checking PNG deflate kernels (no search query); github.com repo page, commits page and README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

Decompression ETC2 599 Mpx/s single-threaded vs 'Nvidia in-driver ETC2 decoder can do only 42.5 Mpx/s' (14x, derived from page data).

The quality comparison image is hosted on imgur, which I did not open. Compiler and flags not stated. Weak entry kept for the keep-and-document rule.
