name: fNBLI (NBLI lossless image codec)
baseline: libpng (via Pillow 10.1.0) and libwebp lossless (via Pillow)
workload: Single-threaded lossless compression and decompression of the CLIC2021 training set (585 RGB 24-bit images, 4 GB) and six other datasets, in the author's Image-Compression-Benchmark shootout.
claimed_speedup: NBLI README (CLIC2021): fNBLI 94.8 MB/s compress and 149.1 MB/s decompress, 29.79% smaller than optipng PNG; Pillow PNG 12.2 and 121.5 MB/s (5.13% larger than optipng); WebP -5 3.7 and 82.8 MB/s (22.53% smaller than optipng). Shootout totals, CLIC2021: fNBLI 43.164 s compress, 27.450 s decompress, 1,337,587,020 bytes vs Pillow PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 s, 33.677 s, 2,003,016,524 bytes and Pillow WebP lossless m5 1112.134 s, 49.442 s, 1,475,908,700 bytes (derived: 7.8x faster encode and 1.2x faster decode than PNG, 26x faster encode and 1.8x faster decode than WebP, with smaller files).
compiler_and_flags: NBLI README build: g++ -O3 -static (MinGW or Linux); the shootout ran the prebuilt fNBLI.exe, which needs AVX2; compiler of that binary not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7 12700H, 16GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10, single-threaded with SIMD allowed
tradeoffs: Custom non-PNG format for 8-bit gray and 24-bit RGB; GPL-3.0 (copyleft); fNBLI needs AVX2. The slower prototype NBLI (-g, 14.7 MB/s compress, 17.0 MB/s decompress) compresses to -30.37% but decodes far slower than PNG. Includes PNG and PNM input.
caveats: Author-run benchmark of the author's own codec; PNG and WebP go through Python Pillow (including process and interpreter overhead per file), not the C libraries directly. The fNBLI source directory src/fNBLI exists (commit 'make fNBLI opensource', 2026-07-18) but the README still links fNBLI.exe and the shootout's format table still marks fNBLI as not open source, so the benchmarked binary may not match the repo source. Compiler flags for the benchmarked binary unknown, hence tier C.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'lossless image compression paper code released outperforms PNG WebP JPEG XL ... SIMD' surfaced NBLI and the Image-Compression-Benchmark shootout

name: gif_load
baseline: giflib 5.2.2 (also stb_image)
workload: Wall-time decode of every frame of 6 synthetic animated GIFs (320x240 x100, 640x480 x200, 1920x1080 x150; flat shapes and incompressible noise), file read into RAM with read() or mmap(), cold and warm page cache.
claimed_speedup: Warm cache: 1.3x-1.7x faster than giflib and 1.4x-2.5x faster than stb_image (e.g. 1080p shapes 668 ms vs giflib stream 1149 ms vs stb_image 1829 ms). Cold cache: 1.3x-1.5x vs giflib on the 3 shape GIFs but 0.83x-0.85x (slower) on the 3 noise GIFs. Author says the 1.3x-1.5x cold claim also holds on real giphy GIFs. Peak memory: one frame plus a 16 KB code table versus giflib slurp 296 MB at 1080p.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5 -O2, Linux 6.4
hardware: CPU model not stated (RAM latency 128 ns, 8 GB/s sequential read, EXT4 cold disk read 342 MB/s)
tradeoffs: Whole file must be in memory before decoding (cannot overlap I/O with decode, which is why cold noise cases lose to giflib). Callback API, header-only, under 300 lines, no libc dependency apart from realloc. Interlaced GIFs are the caller's job to unwind (giflib's DGifSlurp does it). Public-domain dedication (no patent grant).
caveats: The README says 'take everything below with a grain of salt' and that the harness is not published, so the numbers are not reproducible from the repo; synthetic GIFs only; best of two runs. Does not claim to beat stb_image's memory-heavy approach on anything but speed and memory.
found_via: github.com/topics/gif?l=c page listed hidefromkgb/gif_load as 'slim, fast'; README Performance section read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: giflib-turbo
baseline: giflib
workload: GIF LZW decoding through the unchanged giflib API; the decoder uses the output image buffer as the LZW dictionary instead of a linked-list string table.
claimed_speedup: Per search-result snippet of the author's blog post and a repo summary (not opened, see caveats): about 5x faster than giflib on images with a low compression ratio and more than 20x faster on well-compressed images. The repo README itself says only 'A faster drop-in replacement for GIFLIB' with identical function names, parameters and output.
stars_or_usage: 39 stars; drop-in for giflib, which is packaged in vcpkg and Conan
tradeoffs: Uses more RAM than giflib (the author's own description: 'It uses more RAM, but you get more speed'); the README lists possible security vulnerabilities and CPU incompatibilities as not yet tested, and says it may take a long time before big projects adopt it.
caveats: Snippet only: the numbers come from a WebSearch snippet of the author's blog post 'A Big Memory GIF Decoder' (bitbanksoftware.blogspot.com, 2021-03, blocked by the egress proxy and not opened) and of a deepwiki summary (also blocked); the github.com repo page and README carry no numbers, test.c is the only test file and no benchmark script is visible. No CPU, compiler, flags or test images known. Search-summary text also mentioned '2.5x to 30x' overall, which could not be confirmed. Only decoding is claimed. Last commit March 2024 and 10 commits in total.
found_via: giflib is a vcpkg and Conan port; WebSearch 'giflib-turbo GIF decoder faster than giflib SIMD github' surfaced the drop-in replacement; repo page and commits opened on github.com

name: Goofy (realtime DXT1/ETC1 encoder)
baseline: stb_dxt (ryg DXT1, STB_DXT_NORMAL); also rgbcx 1.08, icbc 1.0 and rg_etc1 1.04
workload: Single-thread compression speed in megapixels per second and RGB-PSNR on a test image set (README examples show Kodak kodim17, kodim18 and Lena) using each encoder's fastest or lowest-quality setting.
claimed_speedup: Goofy DXT1 1429 MP/s at 37.02 dB vs rgbcx v1.08 level 0 60 MP/s (40.85 dB), ryg stb_dxt 43 MP/s (40.82 dB), icbc v1.0 24 MP/s (41.00 dB); Goofy ETC1 1221 MP/s (36.30 dB) vs rg_etc1 v1.04 3 MP/s (40.87 dB). Ratios derived from page data: about 24x vs rgbcx, 33x vs stb_dxt, 60x vs icbc, 407x vs rg_etc1.
hardware: i7-7820HQ 2.9 GHz, single thread, fastest of 128 runs
tradeoffs: Speed over quality by design: about 37.0 dB RGB-PSNR for DXT1 versus roughly 40.8-41.0 dB for the compared encoders (only 3.6 dB above the downsample-to-RGB565 baseline at 33.39 dB). One heuristic, DXT1 and ETC1s only, poor on normal maps; DXT5 and ETC2 alpha are future work. Header-only, needs SSE2 (NEON not implemented).
caveats: Compiler and flags are not given. Test code and data are in the repo (test-data and test-results folders) but I did not open them. The comparison is a speed-quality trade, not equal quality: the compared encoders produce 4 dB higher PSNR. The author compares each tool at its fastest setting.
found_via: github.com/topics/texture-compression?l=c%2B%2B page led to SergeyMakeev/Goofy; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Grok JPEG 2000 codec
baseline: OpenJPEG (JPEG 2000); also Kakadu (proprietary, via GDAL JP2KAK)
workload: GDAL workflows reading JPEG 2000 imagery: Spot 6 on network storage, Spot 6 on local storage, and a Pleiades region read, using 16 threads and a GDAL release build.
claimed_speedup: README table (Grok JP2Grok vs Kakadu JP2KAK vs OpenJPEG): Spot 6 (Network Storage) 35.17 s vs 344 s vs 85 s; Spot 6 (Local Storage) 26.92 s vs 30.57 s vs 52.09 s; Pleiades (Region) 0.74 s vs 1.41 s vs 4.28 s.
compiler_and_flags: GDAL release build (compiler and flags not stated)
hardware: Fedora 42, 16 threads (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Strong copyleft: AGPL v3 (network use triggers source obligations), a poor fit for permissive-license projects. Adds HTJ2K, random-access sub-image decoding with TLM and PLT markers, a multi-level tile cache and S3 access, which are features of the whole GDAL workflow measured. Reported to have started as an OpenJPEG fork (per third-party descriptions seen in search snippets); GitHub does not mark it as a fork.
caveats: JPEG 2000 is outside the listed baselines (libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp, libavif); OpenJPEG is the widely used open-source incumbent. First-party end-to-end GDAL timings that include I/O, caching and region reads, not codec-only throughput. CPU model, compiler flags and the benchmark inputs are not given in the README. Kakadu's 344 s network-storage result is far above its 30.57 s local result, which suggests an I/O-pattern effect rather than codec speed (my inference).
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'HTJ2K OpenJPH OpenJPEG Kakadu encoding decoding speed benchmark faster open source library'
WebSearch 'JPEG 2000 HTJ2K codec C++ "faster than OpenJPEG" github' (result listing Grok); opened README, LICENSE and commits page

name: ICBC (high quality SIMD BC1 encoder)
baseline: squish 1.15 and stb_dxt 1.09 (also RGBCX 1.12 and AMD CMP_Core 4.0.4855)
workload: Average PSNR of BC1 encoders against encode time on the Kodim and Waterloo image sets, several quality levels per encoder.
claimed_speedup: Chart only (time axis unlabeled, values read off the chart image and approximate): at the top quality point (PSNR about 30.9) ICBC-AVX512 takes about 5.5 time units versus about 20.6 for RGBCX and about 19.3 for ICBC-Scalar; squish sits at about 7.4 units for PSNR about 30.43 and AMD CMP at about 14.6 units for PSNR about 30.25.
stars_or_usage: 131 stars; the BC1 encoder used by NVTT
tradeoffs: BC1 (DXT1) only, single header, SIMD variants up to AVX-512; quality levels trade encode time for PSNR.
caveats: The result is a PSNR-versus-time chart with no hardware, compiler or time unit stated, and the numbers above are approximate readings of the picture. The speed lead appears at the highest quality settings; at low quality ICBC, RGBCX and stb are close. The README itself says RGBCX is most likely a better choice for a well supported, actively developed library, and RGBCX is already catalogued. Last commit 2022-11-09.
found_via: Texture-compressor shootout search; opened castano/icbc README and doc/kodim-chart.png

name: ImageZero
baseline: PNG (implementation not named; presumably libpng)
workload: Lossless compression and decompression of 24-bit PPM files, natural photos.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Compared to PNG, it compresses 24 bit PPM files about 20 times faster, and decompresses to PPM about 2 times faster, while the compression rate is nearly as good as PNG for natural photos.'
tradeoffs: Own format and API (README calls it 'early work in progress'; neither format nor API fully outlined). Works on 24-bit RGB only; README says it is not suited for flat computer-generated graphics or grayscale images.
caveats: Only a README paragraph: no benchmark code, images, CPU, compiler, flags or PNG library version, so the baseline is inferred (low confidence). Repository has had no commits since 2013, so the comparison predates modern libpng and zlib-ng. Found in the GitHub topic listings for image-compression and image-decoder; I did not open a second benchmark page.
found_via: github.com/topics/image-compression?l=c%2B%2B and github.com/topics/image-decoder?l=c%2B%2B (cfeck/imagezero listed as 'Fast Lossless Color Image Compression Library'); opened the README and commits page

name: jpeg-rusturbo
baseline: image crate JPEG encoder (jpeg-encoder) and decoder (zune-jpeg) as used by the Rust image crate; not libjpeg-turbo
workload: Encoding RGB to 4:2:0 JPEG at q=80 for 1592x1124, 1080p and 4K, single thread and auto threads; decoding the resulting JPEG to RGB on synthetic and natural-like images.
claimed_speedup: Encode 4:2:0 4K single thread: Apple M-series 13.41 ms vs 67.61 ms for image (5.04x); Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL 57.27 ms vs 320.93 ms (5.60x). Encode with threads=auto 4K: 6.83 ms vs 68.47 ms (10.02x) on Apple M, 46.77 ms vs 320.95 ms (6.86x) on Xeon. Decode 4K natural-like: 5.93 ms vs 7.00 ms (1.18x) Apple M, 28.01 ms vs 34.26 ms (1.22x) Xeon; decode at 1592x1124 on Xeon is parity or slightly slower (0.97x to 0.98x).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench with release profile lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1; SIMD build (AVX2 / NEON) versus force-scalar feature; rustc version not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL @ 2.60 GHz, 4 vCPU (AVX2); Apple Silicon M-series developer laptop, 8 cores (exact model not stated), NEON.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; crates.io jpeg-rusturbo 0.9.2 with about 7.8k downloads
tradeoffs: Rust crate with unsafe SIMD kernels (AVX2 and NEON only, AVX-512 and SVE explicitly not planned). Encoder handles baseline and progressive, RGB/gray/CMYK, EXIF/ICC pass-through; decoder handles baseline and progressive Huffman. Optional rayon threading.
caveats: No comparison with libjpeg-turbo or mozjpeg: the baseline is the Rust image crate, whose encoder is scalar, so the 5x to 10x encode win says nothing about libjpeg-turbo. Decode is at rough parity with zune-jpeg (the BENCH.md says so itself). Methodology is one timed batch of 50 iterations after 3 warm-ups with no statistical filtering; Apple M CPU model and rustc version not stated; decode numbers are retained from an older campaign.
found_via: WebSearch: 'pure Rust image decoder faster than libpng libjpeg-turbo libwebp benchmark github' snippet mentioning jpeg-rusturbo, then crates.io API and github.com/naoto256/jpeg-rusturbo plus BENCH.md.

name: jpeg4py (Python libjpeg-turbo wrapper)
language: Python (cffi bindings over the C library libjpeg-turbo)
baseline: Python Pillow Image.open().tobytes() and scipy.misc.imread() JPEG decoding
workload: Decoding JPEG files into numpy arrays through the TurboJPEG API (tjDecompress2), single-threaded and multithreaded.
claimed_speedup: README: 'about 1.3 times faster than Image.open().tobytes() and scipy.misc.imread() in a single thread and up to 9 times faster in multithreaded mode.'
tradeoffs: Decode only (tjInitDecompress, tjDecompressHeader2, tjDecompress2); needs libturbojpeg installed separately. The multithreaded gain comes from releasing the GIL, not from a faster decoder. Python binding, so not usable directly from C++.
caveats: Wrapper of libjpeg-turbo, which is already catalogued, so this duplicates that entry. README was written for Python 2.7/3.4 on Ubuntu 14.04 and names no CPU, library version or benchmark script; the comparison targets are Pillow and scipy of that era. Repository is abandoned (last commit 2018-02-23).
found_via: PyPI JSON API scan (pypi.org/pypi/jpeg4py/json: 'libjpeg-turbo cffi bindings and helper classes'), then repo page and commits on github.com

name: LERC (Limited Error Raster Compression)
baseline: zlib deflate level 9 (labelled 'LZW' in the benchmark document; called through compress2)
workload: Tile-by-tile (1024 max tile) encode and decode of float and 16-bit integer geospatial rasters (4600x4300 float TIFFs, DTED-1 1201x1201 and DTED-2 3601x3601 int16 elevation, multi-band 11/16-bit satellite imagery) against zlib level 9.
claimed_speedup: Lossless 16-bit DTED-2 (MaxZError 0): average encode 231 ms vs 2484 ms and average decode 51 ms vs 130 ms for zlib-9 (about 10.8x and 2.5x, derived from page data). Float rasters (MaxZError 0.01): average encode 0.3 s vs 8.1 s, decode 68 ms vs 424 ms. Multi-spectral lossless: average encode 2.4 s vs 30.5 s, decode 0.7 s vs 1.8 s; the document says 'the much faster encoding speed of 5-10x'. README: encode about 20-30 ms and decode about 5 ms per megapixel per band.
stars_or_usage: 215 stars; vcpkg port lerc and Conan recipe lerc; README says it is used in Esri software
tradeoffs: Special-purpose raster codec for 16-bit and larger or float data with a bounded per-pixel error (MaxZError); lossless only for integer types with MaxZError 0 and only slightly better ratio than zlib there. The README itself says PNG can compress 8-bit data better.
caveats: Benchmark document is from February 2016 and states no CPU, compiler or flags. The baseline is zlib deflate level 9 (not libpng or a tuned PNG encoder). The lossy LERC settings (MaxZError 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 2, 4, 5) are not the same task as lossless zlib, so only the MaxZError 0 columns are like for like. Not a general photographic codec.
found_via: vcpkg port scan (microsoft/vcpkg ports/lerc, description 'rapid encoding and decoding for any pixel type'), then README link to doc/LercBenchmarks_Feb_2016.pdf

name: libjpeg-turbo
baseline: IJG libjpeg (libjpeg 6b reference)
workload: JPEG compression and decompression on systems with common CPU architectures, SIMD-accelerated Huffman and DCT paths.
claimed_speedup: README: 'generally 2-6x as fast as libjpeg, all else being equal'; on systems without SIMD support it 'can still outperform libjpeg by a significant amount' thanks to optimized Huffman coding.
tradeoffs: Drop-in libjpeg API and ABI plus the simpler TurboJPEG API; SIMD per architecture (x86, ARM and others); the README lists performance pitfalls: decompression can drop by as much as 20% (still far above libjpeg) for JPEGs with restart markers, and compression can drop by as much as 40% when the fast integer forward DCT is used at JPEG quality 98 to 100.
caveats: First-party claim with no published methodology, so tier C; this category's own baseline list already names libjpeg-turbo, so it is recorded here against the IJG libjpeg incumbent. Independent runs I opened show it ahead of newer decoders: jpeg-nitro's README table has libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 at 124 ms per image versus stb_image 175 ms and Wuffs 159 ms on an Intel i9, and google/decoder-benchmarks-for-rust has turbojpeg at 84.25 ms versus jpeg-decoder at 126.2 ms on a 2000x3000 image. Neither run uses IJG libjpeg as the baseline.
found_via: Opened libjpeg-turbo README after the 'faster than libjpeg-turbo' search; checked its ChangeLog for other speed numbers

name: libjpeg-turbo-rs
baseline: libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 (decode) and 3.2.0 (encode)
workload: JPEG decode of 64x64 to 3840x2160 images at 4:2:0, 4:2:2, 4:4:4, quality 75, and encode at 640x480 to 1920x1080, Rust vs C in microseconds per image, on x86_64 AVX2 and Apple M1 Pro.
claimed_speedup: README decode table, Intel i5-10400 vs C libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2: time ratios 0.77x (320x240 4:2:0), 0.87x (1280x720 4:2:0), 0.90x (1920x1080 4:2:0), 0.93x (2560x1440), 0.88x (3840x2160), but 1.23x (64x64) and 1.05x (640x480 4:2:0), i.e. about 3 to 23% faster on most sizes. Encode on Zen 3 and Zen 4 runners: stock build is 1.05 to 1.10x C 3.2.0's time at 1080p (slower); the target-cpu=native i5-10400 build is 2 to 7% faster than C 3.1.2. Apple M1 Pro: 0.99 to 1.07x of C.
compiler_and_flags: stock `cargo build --release` (portable runtime dispatch) for decode and the portable encode table; RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native for the supplementary i5-10400 encode table; rustc and C build flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-10400 @ 2.90GHz (turbo off); AMD EPYC 7763 (Zen 3) and Zen 4 GitHub runners; Apple M1 Pro
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust port of libjpeg-turbo with NEON, AVX2, SSE2 and WASM SIMD128 kernels, byte-for-byte cross-validated against C in CI; ships C ABI shims (TurboJPEG 3 and libjpeg-compatible) so C++ can link it. MSRV 1.87. Lossless transforms and progressive supported.
caveats: First-party harness, tiny project (9 stars); the commit page credits Claude as co-author on recent commits. Decode wins are 3 to 23% and mixed (small images lose); the stock portable encoder is slower than C on 1080p, only a target-cpu=native build wins. Compiler versions and C libjpeg-turbo build flags are not stated, so tier C. On Apple M1 Pro it is not faster than C.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'SIMD JPEG encoder decoder AVX2 AVX-512 NEON faster than libjpeg-turbo github open source 2025'

name: lodepng-turbo
baseline: libpng
workload: Baseline PNG decompression using SIMD filters and libdeflate in place of zlib (no workload described).
claimed_speedup: README: 'On x86 and x86-64 or ARM systems, lodepng-turbo is twice as fast as libpng, but it may be slower elsewhere.' No numbers beyond 'twice as fast'.
tradeoffs: Hacked lodepng with libdeflate (git submodule, builds with gcc/clang and GNU make) plus 'depng' prediction routines for unfiltering; accelerates decoding only. Implements both the lodepng API and a TurboPNG API. README itself warns it 'may be slower elsewhere'.
caveats: No benchmark program, methodology, CPU, compiler or data in the repository; the single ratio is first-party. Repository has had no commits since January 2019, so numbers predate current libpng (which has its own SIMD) and libdeflate. The predecessor repository kanryu/simd_lode_png states a goal of 5x libpng but contains no measurements.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' (result kanryu/lodepng-turbo); opened README and commits page

name: MANGO image codecs
baseline: libpng and libjpeg (version not stated in README; possibly libjpeg-turbo)
workload: Decode and encode time in milliseconds of one 2560x1600 and one 4833x5875 PNG, and one 5184x3456 and one 2560x1600 JPEG, against libpng, lodepng, stb, spng, fpng, Wuffs and libjpeg, toojpeg.
claimed_speedup: README table, 2560x1600 PNG: mango decode 3.2 ms vs libpng 57.3 ms (about 18x, derived from page data) and encode 57.2 ms vs 820.5 ms (about 14x, derived). 4833x5875 PNG: decode 53.7 vs 379.5 ms, encode 287.0 vs 14051.3 ms. JPEG 5184x3456: decode 23.3 vs libjpeg 197.8 ms (about 8.5x, derived), encode 18.5 vs 70.1 ms (about 3.8x, derived). JPEG 2560x1600: decode 3.2 vs 32.9 ms, encode 4.3 vs 16.3 ms.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-11800H @ 2.30GHz (PNG tables); Intel Core i9-8950HK @ 2.90GHz (JPEG tables)
tradeoffs: Large C++20 graphics library (vector math, SIMD abstraction, virtual filesystem, Vulkan text) with image codecs inside, not a standalone codec. Mango's PNG encode output is larger than libpng's (3531 KB vs 2843 KB on the first image) and its JPEG output is slightly larger than libjpeg's.
caveats: First-party table with no compiler, flags or thread count stated, and the libjpeg version is unstated (the 90 MP/s libjpeg decode speed suggests an optimised build, but this is not confirmed). Mango's decode may use multiple threads; not stated. In both PNG tables the mango output size equals the quoted input file size (3531 KB and 33598 KB), so the input PNGs may themselves be mango-produced, which could favour its decoder. README quotes a sceptical comment from libspng's author.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'github image codec faster than libjpeg-turbo OR faster than libpng ...' surfaced LibMango as a JPEG codec faster than libjpeg-turbo; README opened
Prior knowledge of C++ image libraries (not surfaced by a search query); opened the t0rakka/mango github.com page, README, license and commits page

name: mozjpeg-rs
baseline: mozjpeg (C encoder, libjpeg-turbo fork with trellis quantization)
workload: Encoding a 2048x2048 (4 MP) image 30 times with trellis quantization (AC + DC) and with Huffman-optimized baseline settings.
claimed_speedup: README: trellis modes 'produce 0.05-0.80% smaller files than C mozjpeg while being 6% faster at 2048x2048'. Table: Trellis (AC + DC) 197 ms vs 210 ms for C mozjpeg ('6% faster'); Baseline (huffman opt) 42 ms vs 9 ms for C mozjpeg ('4.6x slower').
compiler_and_flags: cargo test --release --test bench_2k -- --nocapture, 'release mode with AVX2/NEON'; rustc version and RUSTFLAGS not stated.
tradeoffs: Safe Rust (#![forbid(unsafe_code)]) using the archmage safe-SIMD layer; encoder only. Output is byte-identical to C mozjpeg for baseline and progressive modes; trellis output differs slightly (smaller) unless TrellisMode::MozjpegExact is chosen. Optional fast_color(true) gives about 40% faster RGB to YCbCr at the cost of exact parity.
caveats: The speed win exists only for trellis quantization and is 6% on one image size; the faster-baseline case is 4.6x slower than C mozjpeg (README admits the entropy-coding gap). No CPU model, compiler version or flags beyond 'release'. Baseline is mozjpeg, not libjpeg-turbo or libpng.
found_via: WebSearch: 'mozjpeg pure Rust port benchmark faster than mozjpeg libjpeg-turbo encoder github' returned github.com/imazen/mozjpeg-rs; opened repo, README and commits page.

name: msf_gif
language: C (single header, compiles as C99 or C++98)
baseline: gif.h (Charlie Tangora's single-header encoder, named gif_h in the timings file) and jo_gif
workload: GIF encoding time on the author's test animations in the separate msf_gif-testing repo (workload size not stated in the timings file).
claimed_speedup: README: 'uses SSE where available to encode at hundreds of megabytes a second, several times faster than comparable gif libraries'. timings.txt in msf_gif-testing: jo_gif ~425 seconds, gif_h ~75 seconds, msf_gif ~14 seconds, msf_gif simd ~8 seconds, msf_gif threaded ~4 seconds, msf_gif simd threaded ~2 seconds (about 5x vs gif_h and 30x vs jo_gif, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Uses one fixed constant-quality palette-and-dither scheme per frame instead of adaptive quantization; delta encoding between frames for smaller files. SSE on x86 only (NEON listed as a TODO). Public domain, also available under MIT.
caveats: The timings file is a four-line note with no hardware, input set, compiler or flags, so it is a bare first-party number; it does not say which gif.h the label gif_h refers to (presumably Charlie Tangora's). A gifski comparison is a TODO in the author's notes. The mix of MIT and public-domain dedication carries no patent grant.
found_via: github.com/topics/gif?l=c page listed notnullnotvoid/msf_gif; README plus the linked msf_gif-testing repo timings.txt read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: mtpng (parallel PNG encoder with C API)
baseline: libpng
workload: Re-encoding a dual-4K screenshot PNG at default options, single-threaded and multi-threaded, compared with libpng built by gcc and clang.
claimed_speedup: docs/perf.md old data (MacBook Pro 13in 2015, Core i7 3.1 GHz, Linux x86_64): libpng gcc 850 ms, libpng clang 900 ms, mtpng 1 thread 555 ms (1.5x vs libpng gcc, derived from page data), 2 threads 302 ms (2.8x derived), 4 threads 248 ms (3.4x derived). README: single-threaded about 30-40% faster than libpng (Rust 1.29.0, Sept 2018), 'multiple threads consistently beats libpng by a lot'. 2026 data lists only mtpng times (e.g. Apple M3 Max 23 ms at 16 threads, 237 ms at 1 thread; Ryzen 9 5950X 25 ms at 32 threads, 301 ms at 1 thread).
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release (Rust); libpng built with gcc or clang, versions and zlib not stated
hardware: MacBook Pro 13in 2015, 5th-gen Core i7 3.1 GHz, 2 cores plus Hyper-Threading (libpng comparison); several newer machines for mtpng-only timings
tradeoffs: Encoder only; input must be pre-packed pixels. Compression ratio is a tiny fraction worse than libpng at the default 256 KiB chunk size (closer with larger chunks). Files under 128 KiB uncompressed see no threading gain. Rust library with a C API that the README says is still unstable; pulls libz_sys. Small-file and ancillary-chunk support needs work.
caveats: perf.md itself says '@fixme how did I measure those libpng times? need to recreate that', so the libpng baseline numbers are from 2015-2018 and unverified; the 2026 section has no libpng column. Third-party libpng version and zlib build are unstated.
found_via: github.com/topics/png-encoder page listed brion/mtpng; README and docs/perf.md read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: nativewebp
baseline: Go standard library image/png encoder at png.BestCompression
workload: Encoding five images from Google's WebP lossless gallery with the lossless-only nativewebp encoder at nativewebp.BestCompression versus image/png at png.BestCompression, reported in ns/op together with output size.
claimed_speedup: README: encoder is 'approximately 50% faster' than the standard Go PNG encoder and produces smaller files. Per image (PNG ns/op vs nativewebp ns/op): 42,945,049 vs 35,413,726 (17% faster, 21% smaller file); 98,509,399 vs 42,626,779 (57% faster, 24% smaller); 178,205,535 vs 96,800,750 (46% faster, 19% smaller); 29,088,555 vs 19,877,708 (32% faster, 26% smaller); 63,423,995 vs 27,813,126 (56% faster, 14% smaller).
compiler_and_flags: Go benchmark (ns/op); Go version and flags not stated.
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no cgo or libwebp. Encodes only lossless WebP (VP8L) and animations; decoding is a wrapper around golang.org/x/image/webp. Not a lossy encoder.
caveats: README calls it 'a quick benchmark': five gallery images, no hardware or Go version, no benchmark code location named. The comparison is against Go's own PNG encoder, not libwebp, libpng or any C codec, so it does not show nativewebp beating libwebp (which compresses and encodes differently).
found_via: GitHub: opened github.com/HugoSmits86/nativewebp directly while checking Go WebP libraries (Go row of the any-language assignment); read README and commits page.

name: nvavif-py
baseline: Pillow with pillow-avif-plugin (libavif/libaom decode) and software AV1 encoders (libaom, rav1e, SVT-AV1) for encode
workload: Decoding a 5184x3456 AVIF to a NumPy array including disk read, and encoding AVIF with NVIDIA NVENC versus software AV1 encoders.
claimed_speedup: README decode table: nvavif_py.decode_file() ~80 ms vs Pillow (pillow-avif-plugin) ~360 ms (a second table says 320 ms), OpenCV ~280 ms, imageio + av ~400 ms; 'nvavif_py is 3-4x faster than standard tools'. Encode: NVENC 'milliseconds per image' versus software 'dozens of seconds per image', '200x'.
tradeoffs: PyO3 Rust extension wrapping dav1d (decode, fixed-point YUV to RGB, rayon), rav1e (CPU encode fallback) and NVENC AV1 hardware encode via ffmpeg-next; GPU encode needs an RTX 40/50-series (Ada Lovelace or Blackwell) card. Pillow save plugin included.
caveats: Numbers have no stated hardware, library versions, thread counts or method, and the two README tables disagree (320 ms vs 360 ms for Pillow). Single commit ('init'), zero stars. The decode gain is mostly a backend choice (dav1d, multithreaded) versus a plugin the README says uses libaom, so it is largely a dav1d wrapper effect, and the NVENC 'dozens of seconds versus milliseconds' encode comparison is hardware versus software at unmatched quality settings. Likely folds into the dav1d, rav1e and libavif entries.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/avif-decoder listing flagged imbecility/nvavif-py ('High-performance Python library for encoding/decoding AVIF images using hardware acceleration'); opened repo, README and commits page.

name: oss-nvjpg
baseline: libjpeg-turbo
workload: Baseline JPEG decode to an RGB surface, 720x1080 (70 KiB file) and 3200x1800 (1.6 MiB file), average of 1000 iterations, on a Tegra X1 (Aarch64 Cortex-A57 at 2.091 GHz).
claimed_speedup: NVJPG hardware decoder: 2.036 ms vs libjpeg-turbo 6.127 ms (70 KiB image) and 15.997 ms vs 66.341 ms (1.6 MiB image); ratios about 3.0x and 4.1x (derived from page data). Also listed: stb_image with NEON 16.512 / 158.474 ms, Python-pillow 11.688 / 114.918 ms, nanoJPEG 48.299 / 531.575 ms.
hardware: Nvidia Tegra X1 SoC, Aarch64 Cortex-A57 at max 2.091 GHz (hardware JPEG block NVJPG)
tradeoffs: Drives the Tegra X1 hardware JPEG block (NVJPG) through the Host1x interface, so it only runs on Tegra X1 class devices (for example Nintendo Switch homebrew with devkitA64). Baseline JPEG only: progressive and arithmetic coded files return an error. Hardware YUV to RGB conversion and downscaling by up to 8. Requires C++20. GPL-3.0 license limits reuse in permissive projects.
caveats: First-party README table only; no compiler, flags or libjpeg-turbo version stated, and the README does not say whether the timing harness ships in the repo (examples are built separately). Two test images only. The speedup comes from dedicated hardware, not from a better software algorithm, so it does not transfer to other CPUs. Cortex-A57 libjpeg-turbo number presumably uses NEON but this is not stated.
found_via: Blogs / talks query: 'GPUJPEG OR nvImageCodec JPEG decode throughput vs libjpeg-turbo images per second github benchmark' surfaced the oss-nvjpg reference; README opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: oxipng
baseline: OptiPNG
workload: Lossless PNG optimization of single test images (d3js.org.png, powertoys.png) by an independent blog comparison; wall-clock time and size reduction at default and maximum levels.
claimed_speedup: From the blog, via search snippet: d3js.org.png default level oxipng 0.764 s for 29.14% reduction versus optipng 2.638 s for 25.42% (about 3.5x faster, derived); powertoys.png oxipng 0.266 s for 17.62% versus optipng 0.960 s for 5.85% (about 3.6x faster, derived); at maximum settings oxipng --opt max --zopfli 28.896 s for 30.25% versus optipng -o 7 -strip all 32.800 s for 25.53%.
tradeoffs: Rust command-line tool and library (not a C or C++ API); multithreaded by design, the README says it began as a Rust rewrite of OptiPNG to add multithreading. Optimizes existing PNG/APNG files, it is not a general encoder. Higher levels and --zopfli are slow.
caveats: Snippet only: op111.net is blocked from this environment, so the numbers are copied from a search-result summary and not checked against the page; the oxipng README links the blog as an independent benchmark 'with permission by the author'. Hardware, versions and flags unknown. The speed gain is largely multithreading versus single-threaded OptiPNG, and it is also a better optimizer at the same level, so the comparison mixes time and size.
found_via: WebSearch 'oxipng and friends: A comparison of PNG optimization tools'; oxipng README Benchmarks section links the blog

name: Pfim
baseline: FreeImage, DevIL and ImageMagick (native C/C++ libraries driven through .NET wrappers), plus managed Targa/DDS decoders (TargaImage, ImageFormats, StbSharp, TgaSharpLib)
workload: Decoding one 120x120 image stored as 3 Targa variants (24-bit RLE, 32-bit RLE, 32-bit raw) and 4 DDS variants (32-bit, DXT1, DXT3, DXT5), measured with BenchmarkDotNet as mean time per decode.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Pfim is hands down the fastest targa decoder. More than 10x faster than the closest competitor'; for DDS 'one of the fastest if not the fastest', first everywhere except DXT5 where it is 1% slower. From TargaBenchmark-report.csv (Mean column, unit not printed, BenchmarkDotNet default is ns): 24bit-rle.tga Pfim 5,083.1 vs FreeImage 65,756.5 vs DevILSharp 47,792.0 (about 12.9x and 9.4x, derived from page data); 32bit.tga Pfim 3,655.9 vs DevILSharp 52,740.6 (about 14.4x, derived from page data). DdsBenchmark-report.csv: 32bit.dds Pfim 1,569.2 vs DevILSharp 115,072.4; dxt1.dds Pfim 46,734.1 vs FreeImage 75,354.5; dxt5.dds Pfim 93,732.4 vs FreeImage 92,683.4 (Pfim slightly slower).
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet; CSV columns show Runtime=Clr, Jit=RyuJit, Platform=X64; release build flags and .NET Framework version not stated in the numbers file.
tradeoffs: .NET library that decodes only Targa (TGA) and DirectDraw Surface (DDS) files; no PNG/JPEG/WebP. Returns raw pixel data with optional pooled allocator, so display needs extra glue (System.Drawing, ImageSharp, WPF samples in the README).
caveats: One 120x120 test image per format, so per-call fixed costs dominate. The CSV carries no CPU model. DevIL, FreeImage and ImageMagick are called through .NET wrapper libraries, so interop overhead is included in their times. README claim 'more than 10x faster than the closest competitor' does not hold for 24bit-rle.tga against DevILSharp (9.4x, derived from page data). Competitor versions are from the 0.10.0 era (DevIL 0.2.19, FreeImage 4.3.6, ImageMagick 7.12.0). Baselines are not libjpeg-turbo/libpng/libwebp/libavif, so the result says little about mainstream codecs.
found_via: GitHub: opened github.com/nickbabcock/Pfim (C# row of the any-language assignment) and its analysis/ directory (TargaBenchmark-report.csv, DdsBenchmark-report.csv).

name: pngenc
baseline: libpng 1.6 (with zlib)
workload: Encode one 1920x1080 24-bit image to PNG in three low-compression modes (uncompressed, Huffman-only, RLE).
claimed_speedup: README table (ms, libpng 1.6 vs pngenc 1 thread vs pngenc multi-threaded): Uncompressed 9 vs 0.8 vs 0.2; Huffman Only 82 vs 7.3 vs 1.2; RLE 84 vs 30 vs 4. README says 'up to an order of magnitude faster' at the same compression rates in those modes.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X
tradeoffs: Encoder only. Supports only uncompressed, Huffman-only and RLE modes (full LZ77 is 'N/A'), so it does not replace libpng at default compression levels. Needs OpenMP for the multi-threaded numbers; tested with gcc/mingw, clang and MSVC. Author calls it a hobby project; the CRC32 code is adapted from Mark Adler under a zlib-compatible license.
caveats: Single first-party table, one image and one CPU; compiler, flags and benchmark harness are not stated. The comparison is against libpng's low-effort strategies (Z_HUFFMAN_ONLY, Z_RLE) which the README itself calls a valid trade-off. No libpng-at-default-level comparison is given for any mode that pngenc supports.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' (result GregorBudweiser/pngenc); opened readme.md, LICENSE and commits page

name: PngEncoder (Java)
baseline: javax.imageio PNG writer (ImageIO, JDK built-in encoder)
workload: Encoding BufferedImages to PNG at the default compression level 9: a random 1024x1024 image, a 2121x350 logo and a 4900x6000 fashion photograph, reported as images encoded per second.
claimed_speedup: README: 'About 5 times faster than ImageIO (on a computer with 8 logical cores)'. Table (images encoded per second, PngEncoder vs ImageIO): random1024x1024 36.324 vs 5.150 (7.1x), logo2121x350 127.034 vs 24.857 (5.1x), looklet4900x6000 0.159 vs 0.029 (5.5x). Lowering the compression level adds up to 2.3x more speed at the cost of about 2.5x larger files (level 1) according to the README speed-versus-size table.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark source is PngEncoderBenchmarkPngEncoderVsImageIO.java in the repo; JDK version and JVM flags not stated (project targets Java 8).
hardware: A computer with 8 logical cores (CPU model not stated).
stars_or_usage: 46 stars; used in production at Looklet per README
tradeoffs: Pure Java; speedup comes mainly from multithreaded DEFLATE over blocks, so output is about 2% larger than ImageIO at the same level. Optional predictor encoding and indexed output give smaller files at a speed cost. Encoder only.
caveats: Speedup is almost entirely multithreading: README says a single-core machine will not see a significant gain. CPU model, JDK version and warm-up method are not stated, and the benchmark is the project's own. Baseline is the JDK ImageIO writer, not libpng; the Java wrapper fpng-java (not reported here) reports much larger gains over ImageIO by calling the native fpng library.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Java image codec library faster than ImageIO benchmark PNG JPEG WebP encoder decoder github "faster than"' returned github.com/pngencoder/pngencoder.

name: ptpng
baseline: libpng with zlib-ng 2.2.4 (ZLIB_COMPAT); for the encoder also stock zlib level 6 and zlib-ng level 6
workload: PNG decode (27 cases across native, RGB8 and RGBA8 output) and encode (nine generated fixtures: gradients, graphics, noise) on five CI platforms, median of alternating rounds.
claimed_speedup: README: decoder geometric-mean speedup over libpng + zlib-ng 2.2.4 across 27 cases is 1.80x Linux x64, 1.64x Windows x64, 1.59x Linux ARM64, 1.62x macOS ARM64 and 1.46x Windows ARM64 (30 Sep 2026 run). Encoder (after 1 Oct change) averages 2.25-2.98x stock zlib level 6 and 1.14-1.52x zlib-ng, with files at most 2.4% larger than zlib-ng level 6.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build; nightly workflow matrix uses gcc, clang and MSVC cl (versions not stated); PERFORMANCE.md quotes -O3 for paired runs and MSVC /O2 for one local run
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (Windows x64 runner, four logical CPUs) for the 30 Sep snapshot; Intel i7-1355U for local runs; Neoverse-N2 for Linux ARM64 (PERFORMANCE.md)
tradeoffs: No LICENSE file found at the repo root (raw.githubusercontent.com returned 404 for LICENSE, LICENSE.md and LICENSE.txt) and the README has no license section, so reuse rights are unclear. Single-threaded; library calls must be serialized across threads (shared tables and dispatch state). Encoder writes non-interlaced PNG without palette, packed-sample or metadata support. C11 core with a header-only C++17/20 wrapper; AVX2/SSE2 on x86 and NEON on ARM64.
caveats: Very new repository (0 stars; commit activity visible from 2026-09-24 and PERFORMANCE.md is titled 'September-October 2026'); numbers change nightly and the README says compare ratios only within a run. Fixtures are synthetic (gradients, graphics, random noise) and the project itself says they do not establish a fastest-in-the-world claim. Decoder loses on some Windows cases (26/27) and the new encoder loses to zlib-ng level 6 in several fixtures (for example 0.76x on photo_rgb8 in the local i7-1355U table per PERFORMANCE.md). Compiler versions are not stated, so a verifier who finds them in CI logs could promote this to tier A.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' (result bojosos/ptpng); opened README, PERFORMANCE.md, CI workflows and commits page

name: pyspng (Python libspng wrapper)
language: Python (pybind11 extension over the C library libspng)
baseline: Python Pillow PNG loading (libpng with zlib)
workload: Loading uncompressed (PNG compression level 0) PNG files into numpy arrays, aimed at machine-learning datasets.
claimed_speedup: README and PyPI page: 'Synthetic benchmarks indicate pyspng to be roughly 2-3x faster in loading uncompressed PNGs than the Python Pillow library.'
stars_or_usage: 12 stars; PyPI package pyspng (a fork, pyspng-seunglab, adds progressive decoding)
tradeoffs: Decode only, no image manipulation. Python binding, so not directly usable from C++; the C++ route is libspng itself. LICENSE file is BSD-3-Clause text taken from the pybind11 template.
caveats: Thin wrapper of libspng, which is already catalogued, so this mostly duplicates that entry; the claim is only about uncompressed PNGs and names no CPU, compiler, Pillow version or benchmark script (none is visible in the repo). Treat as supporting evidence for libspng rather than a separate codec.
found_via: PyPI JSON API scan of image-codec packages (pypi.org/pypi/pyspng/json: 'Fast libspng-based PNG decoder'), then the repo page and commits on github.com

name: qoi (qoi-rust)
baseline: QOI reference C implementation (phoboslab/qoi qoi.h, commit 8d35d93)
workload: Encode and decode of 2846 PNG images from the QOI benchmark suite (1.32 GPixels, 4.46 GB of raw pixels), single run per codec.
claimed_speedup: Decode 427.4 Mp/s versus 282.9 Mp/s for qoi.h and encode 290.0 Mp/s versus 225.3 Mp/s (1477.7 versus 978.3 MB/s decode, 1002.9 versus 778.9 MB/s encode), about 1.5x decode and 1.3x encode (derived from page data).

caveats: First-party numbers with the suite public but no compiler, flags or rustc version, and one machine (Apple M1). Compares only against the QOI reference, not against libpng, so it says nothing about the category baselines. The README says it is the fastest of the Rust QOI crates but gives no table for the others.
found_via: WebSearch 'QOI encoder decoder AVX2 SIMD faster than reference qoi benchmark github results'

name: qoixx
baseline: qoi.h (reference QOI implementation, phoboslab/qoi)
workload: QOI encode and decode of the QOI benchmark suite (grand total, 20 iterations), ms and megapixels per second, on seven CPUs.
claimed_speedup: README: on Intel Core i9-10900 (g++ 11.1.0) qoi decodes in 2.2389 ms (207.326 mpps) and encodes in 2.5434 ms (182.504 mpps) vs qoixx 1.3477 ms (344.431 mpps) and 1.5255 ms (304.280 mpps), about 1.7x faster in both directions (derived from page data); similar gains on Ryzen 7 2700X, Ryzen 7 3800X, Ryzen 9 3950X, AWS Graviton3, Kryo 585 and Apple M1 Max.
compiler_and_flags: g++ versions listed per CPU, 11.0.0 to 12.0.0 (11.1.0 on the i9-10900); optimization flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i9-10900; AMD Ryzen 7 2700X; Ryzen 7 3800X; Ryzen 9 3950X; AWS Graviton3; Qualcomm Kryo 585; Apple M1 Max
tradeoffs: Single-header C++20 QOI codec with SIMD encoder (AVX2, SVE or NEON, scalar fallback via QOIXX_NO_SIMD). Decoder is optimized scalar and 'with some input, original implementation is faster'. Output size is identical to qoi.h (463 KB total). Decoder built with MSVC is not fast per the FAQ.
caveats: Baseline is qoi.h, not libpng/libwebp, so this only qualifies indirectly: see the QOI entry for qoi.h vs libpng (about 27x encode, 3.4x decode in nigeltao/qoir's run). Optimization flags and benchmark program are not stated in the README; first-party numbers.
found_via: github.com/topics/image-compression?l=c%2B%2B (wx257osn2/qoixx listed as 'Single Header Quite Fast QOI Implementation written in C++20'); opened README, LICENSE and commits page

name: refreshed-astc-encoder
baseline: Mali GPU Texture Compression Tool astcenc binary (32-bit) and ARM astc-encoder official repo build (64-bit, 2015 era)
workload: ASTC compression time of turret_diffuse_map.png at five speed presets (veryfast to exhaustive).
claimed_speedup: 'about 2x faster than the Mali TCT binary and about 1.5x faster than the one from official repo'. Table (seconds, Mali TCT / astcenc / refreshed): veryfast 0.41/0.39/0.19; fast 1.04/0.86/0.40; medium 6.11/4.36/3.20; thorough 22.90/14.98/11.54; exhaustive 52.56/30.99/25.23. Derived from page data: 1.23x-2.15x vs official astcenc and 1.91x-2.60x vs Mali TCT across the five presets.
hardware: Intel Core i5 760
license: ARM ASTC Codec End User Licence Agreement (license.txt, not OSI)
stars_or_usage: 1 star (fork chain: ARM-software/astc-encoder, then Kirpich30000, then abusenius)

Single image, one CPU, no flags. Licence is a custom EULA, so treat as reference only. An identical README is in the abusenius/refreshed-astc-encoder fork.

name: rusty_png
baseline: FFmpeg 8.1.2 PNG decoder and encoder (libavcodec)
workload: PNG decode to rgb24 on 5 admissible images, end-to-end PNG encode from raw pixels (CLIC professional photographs, Derf/xiph video frames) and output size on 9 real graphics (screenshots, charts, diagrams, logos), measured in on-core CPU cycles on one pinned core with ABBA interleaving.
claimed_speedup: README: decode per core '2.55-2.89x faster (median 2.60x)' than FFmpeg; encode wall clock multi-core '2.11-3.06x faster, 0.1-0.2% smaller' (parallel feature, multi-core against FFmpeg's single-threaded encoder); encode per core 0.94-1.05x on CLIC photographs and 0.86-0.91x on Derf video frames (parity to slower); graphics size -6.1% (was +115.6%).
compiler_and_flags: Optional features zlib-rs (on by default) and parallel; compiler version and flags not stated in the README (WHYS.md holds the measurement history).
hardware: 'The same machine', one pinned core each; CPU model not stated.
stars_or_usage: 1 star; README reports 995 active installs through a browser-based file converter
tradeoffs: Performance fork of image-png 0.17.16 for use inside the remade_ffmpeg_rs project: swaps miniz_oxide for flate2's pure-Rust zlib-rs backend, adds multi-threaded DEFLATE for a single image, adaptive filtering for graphics, and memory reductions. Pure Rust, no C.
caveats: Baseline is FFmpeg's PNG codec, not libpng. The decode win is most likely inherited from upstream image-png (already listed) rather than fork changes; the README does not separate the two. The 2-3x encode figure compares multi-core to FFmpeg's single-threaded encoder, and per-core encode is parity or about 13% slower on video frames. Cycle counts exclude process launch; CPU model, rustc version and flags are not stated; Repo created 2026-08-01 by importing a crate from remade_ffmpeg_rs.
found_via: WebSearch: 'fast PNG OR JPEG OR WebP encoder Rust OR Zig OR Nim crate "faster than libpng" ...' returned the repo title 'Decodes 2.7-2.9x faster than FFmpeg'; opened repo, README, commits page.

name: TinyTIFF
baseline: libTIFF (libtiff 3.8.2 and 4.6.0)
workload: Writing many small uncompressed 16-bit frames (64x64, 10 to >100000 frames) and frames of 64x64 to 4096x4096 into one multi-frame TIFF, compared with libTIFF and with raw fwrite(), using the repo's tests/tinytiffwriter_speedtest program.
claimed_speedup: README: 'significantly faster than libTIFF, especially in writing large multi-frame TIFFs'; on an SSD 'still significantly (1.5-3x ...) faster than libTIFF' over frame count and 'faster than libTIFF by a factor of 1.5-5x' over frame size; on a hard disk libTIFF per-frame write time grows with frame count while TinyTIFFWriter stays close to fwrite().
compiler_and_flags: Release builds (32-bit on the Win10 run, 64-bit on the Win11 run); compiler and flags not stated
hardware: Ryzen 5 3600+, Win10, hard disk, libTiff 3.8.2; Ryzen 7 5800H, Win11, SSD, libTiff 4.6.0
tradeoffs: Basic TIFF only: uncompressed pixel data, limited tag set and pixel formats; the writer pre-reserves a fixed header block per frame. LGPL-3.0 licence.
caveats: Speedups are read from log-scale charts (PNG images) and quoted from README prose; the exact per-run numbers are not in text. The hard-disk run uses libTiff 3.8.2, a very old release, and a 32-bit build; only the SSD run uses libTiff 4.6.0. Write-side only: no read-speed comparison. The workload is many tiny frames, where libTIFF's per-directory overhead dominates; for few large frames the README says libTIFF is in the same range. Compiler and flags are not stated, so not tier A.
found_via: vcpkg port scan (microsoft/vcpkg ports/tinytiff, description 'Lightweight TIFF reader/writer library'), then raw README on raw.githubusercontent.com

name: wpd (WebP decoder)
language: Rust with x86 assembly, C ABI (wpd.h)
baseline: libwebp (libwebpdecoder built from the pinned Meson subproject)
workload: Decode time (hyperfine, 3 warmup, 20 runs, single thread, output to /dev/null with format conversion) of 7 test WebP files: lossy, lossy with alpha, lossless and animated, compared with libwebp and the image-webp crate.
claimed_speedup: README table (libwebp ms / wpd ms): lossy.webp YUV420P 180.40/173.56 = 1.04x; simplelf-lossy.webp 174.43/162.07 = 1.08x; anim_yuv.webp RGBA 190.90/169.18 = 1.13x; lossless.webp RGBA 195.75/111.27 = 1.76x; anim_rgb.webp 104.47/62.56 = 1.67x; a_lossy.webp YUVA420P 50.70/36.38 = 1.39x; anim_yuva.webp RGBA 494.37/374.46 = 1.32x. image-webp crate is slower than libwebp on the same files (e.g. lossless 231.50 ms, anim_yuva 776.54 ms).

tradeoffs: Decoder only. Needs the Rust toolchain plus nasm on x86 (Meson build). Assembly is on by default; building with -Denable_asm=false gives memory-safety guarantees at the cost of speed. C API in include/wpd.h, installs static and shared libraries plus wpd.pc, so it is callable from C++. Streaming and cropping/scaling options exist.
caveats: The README table does not name the CPU (it says 'CPU affinity above' but the machine line is gone), so the tier stops at C although scripts/bench.sh is public. Test files live in a separate repo (halidecx/wpd-test-data). Lossy gains are small (1.04x-1.08x); the larger wins are lossless and animation. The README was reformatted on 2026-10-01 and the benchmark commit is dated 2026-10-03, so the numbers are very fresh; a search snippet seen earlier in the session quoted larger ratios (2.38x-4.56x) that no longer appear on the page, so only the current README table is reported. libwebp threading is off in the default single-thread run (THREADS=1).
found_via: WebSearch 'libwebp faster alternative WebP decoder encoder SIMD "faster than libwebp" github' surfaced halidecx/wpd; README and scripts/bench.sh read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: zenjpeg
baseline: libjpeg-turbo (mozjpeg-sys 2.2 with nasm_simd, C+NASM)
workload: JPEG decode throughput on 10 CID22 photos (baseline 4:2:0 and progressive) and parallel decode of baseline JPEGs with restart markers (DRI) at 1024, 2048 and 4096 pixels, zenbench interleaved A/B runs.
claimed_speedup: README: baseline 4:2:0 decode 73.8 MiB/s (default Triangle upsampling) vs libjpeg-turbo 78.1 MiB/s (0.94x, slower) and 80.4 MiB/s with NearestNeighbor upsampling (1.03x); progressive decode 46 vs 34 MiB/s (1.35x faster); parallel decode with DRI: 1.56 vs 3.86 ms at 1024, 3.05 vs 15.8 ms at 2048, 8.74 vs 65.3 ms at 4096 (about 2.5x, 5.2x, 7.5x faster, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: cargo --release, default target, no -C target-cpu=native, runtime SIMD dispatch; rustc version not recorded in the benchmarks README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (WSL2)
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 or paid commercial licence. Pure Rust, so C++ needs bindings. Baseline decode is slightly slower than libjpeg-turbo with libjpeg-compatible upsampling; the large win needs restart markers (DRI) and the parallel feature (multi-threaded versus single-threaded libjpeg-turbo). Decoder API is prerelease. Encoder lands within about 15 to 20% of jpegli at matched quality.
caveats: First-party benchmark. The comparison target is mozjpeg-sys 2.2 (libjpeg-turbo-derived), not stock libjpeg-turbo. Parallel numbers compare multi-threaded zenjpeg against single-threaded libjpeg-turbo. rustc version not recorded. Baseline-JPEG single-thread decode is not faster. Tiny project (15 stars).
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'imazen zenjpeg zenpng zenwebp faster than libjpeg-turbo libwebp libpng benchmark'

name: zenwebp
baseline: libwebp (C reference)
workload: WebP lossless and lossy encode speed and lossy and lossless decode speed in single-threaded zenbench A/B runs against libwebp (webp 0.3.1 / libwebp-sys 0.14) on a 14-image corpus (CLIC2025 photos, screenshots, CID22).
claimed_speedup: README: lossless encoder method 6 is 2.6x faster than libwebp at 1.01x size (132 ms vs 340 ms on a 512x512 photo, docs/PERFORMANCE.md); lossy encoder method 4 is 1.35x faster at 1.01x size; lossy decode 1.09 to 1.12x faster on 2K photos and 1.06 to 1.14x on screenshots; lossless decode 1.23 to 1.31x on screenshots. Lossless methods 2 to 4 are near parity (1.03x).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench, default target, no -C target-cpu=native, runtime SIMD dispatch; rustc version not stated
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 or paid commercial licence. Pure Rust, no_std capable, bit-exact lossy decoder vs libwebp (0 pixel diffs on 12,825 files per README). Lossless method 0 is 2.4x slower than libwebp. Files within 1 to 5% of libwebp's size.
caveats: Internal contradiction: docs/PERFORMANCE.md (dated 2026-03-26) lists lossy decode as 1.14 to 2.22x SLOWER than libwebp (e.g. 223 vs 496 MPix/s on a 4K screenshot), while the newer README claims 1.06 to 1.14x faster; the README numbers may postdate a rewrite but this is not verified. No CPU model is stated in the files read. Only the lossless encoder method 6 win is consistent across both pages. First-party benchmark.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'imazen zenjpeg zenpng zenwebp faster than libjpeg-turbo libwebp libpng benchmark'

name: zune-png (zune-image workspace)
language: Rust (C bindings via the zune-capi crate)
baseline: libspng (spng); libpng is not measured in the table
workload: Criterion decode benchmarks of PNG files: 16 bpp, baseline 8-bit, interlaced 8 bpp and palette images, zune-png versus image-rs/png and spng.
claimed_speedup: benchmarks/benchmark-results.md (ms, spng vs zune-png): baseline 297.4 vs 135.0 (spng 2.20x slower, as printed); interlaced 8bpp 378.0 vs 139.7 (2.71x, as printed); 16 bpp 541.2 vs 186.3 (2.9x, derived from page data); palette 53.59 vs 35.21 (1.5x, derived from page data). image-rs/png is the winner on 16 bpp and palette images.
compiler_and_flags: Rust release profile via cargo bench (criterion); flags not stated in the results file
hardware: A Darwin (macOS) machine; the CPU model is not given
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust decoders with minimal unsafe (only SIMD intrinsics); C access only through the separate zune-capi crate, so it is not a drop-in libpng or spng replacement for C++ code. The workspace also contains zune-jpeg, zune-inflate, zune-qoi, zune-heif and image filters.
caveats: Single results file, Apple hardware, no CPU model, results are criterion timings on the maintainer's file set. In the same file zune-jpeg is slower than mozjpeg on most cases (1.1x-1.3x slower on baseline and subsampled decodes, about 1.0x-1.1x faster only on progressive), and zune-inflate is slower than libdeflate (1.5x-1.7x), so the claim holds for PNG against spng, not for JPEG. The README itself only promises 'on par with or better than reference libraries'. Rust, outside the C++ language filter unless the C API is used.
found_via: Guessed owner/repo while checking READMEs of Rust image decoders (jxl-rs, jxl-oxide, rav1d, image-webp, zune-image); zune-image README linked benchmarks/benchmark-results.md, read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Basis Universal (bc7f and etc1f real-time encoders)
baseline: bc7e.ispc level 1 (BC7) and etcpak (ETC1)
workload: Analytical, non-SIMD real-time BC7 (bc7f) and ETC1 (etc1f) block encoders in the transcoder module; no benchmark figures given.
claimed_speedup: Wiki: 'Even without any SIMD, bc7f is several times faster than our bc7e.ispc encoder at level 1, with a slightly lower average PSNR'; 'etc1f is significantly faster and more portable than etcpak'. No numbers.

name: @napi-rs/canvas
language: Rust (Skia binding for Node.js via Node-API)
baseline: node-canvas (the npm 'canvas' package v3.2.3, which renders with Cairo)
workload: Same samizdatco/canvas-benchmarks Node.js canvas scripts as skia-canvas (Path2D drawing, Bezier curves, dense line chart, SVG to PNG, scale/rotate images, gradients, text, PDF to PNG, get/put ImageData, cold start), measured against the Cairo-based canvas package.
claimed_speedup: Relative to canvas (Cairo) = 1.0x, @napi-rs/canvas v1.0.10: Path2D 99 ms vs 133 ms = 1.3x; Bezier curves 181 ms vs 418 ms = 2.3x; dense line chart 79 ms vs 135 ms = 1.7x; SVG to PNG 1.4x; scale/rotate images 193 ms vs 819 ms = 4.2x; gradients 25 ms vs 57 ms = 2.3x; text 19 ms vs 24 ms = 1.2x; PDF to PNG 1.1x; get/put ImageData 283 ms vs 272 ms (no gain, 1.0x); cold start 71 ms vs 108 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Node 24.6.0; prebuilt npm packages @napi-rs/canvas v1.0.10 and canvas v3.2.3; native build flags not stated on the results page

The project's own README also reports 'Draw a House and export to PNG' at 68 ops/s versus node-canvas 60 ops/s and 'Draw Gradient and export to PNG' at 66 versus 56 ops/s on an Apple M3 Max (about 1.13x and 1.18x, derived from page data); the README labels its own row '@napi-rs/skia', an older package name. Speedup mainly reflects Skia versus Cairo, and several rows are near parity (get/put ImageData 1.0x, PDF to PNG 1.1x, text 1.2x). Tier A is generous: prebuilt npm binaries, so compiler and flags are not stated.

name: skia-canvas
baseline: node-canvas (the npm 'canvas' package v3.2.3, which renders with Cairo)
workload: Node.js Canvas 2D API test scripts in the samizdatco/canvas-benchmarks repo (Path2D drawing, Bezier curves, dense line chart, SVG to PNG/SVG/PDF, PDF to PNG, scale/rotate images, get/put ImageData, gradients, text, cold start), each timed over 20-250 iterations with the Cairo-based canvas package as the 1.0x baseline.
claimed_speedup: Relative to canvas (Cairo) = 1.0x, skia-canvas serial / async: Path2D 45 ms vs 133 ms = 3.0x / 20 ms = 6.7x; Bezier curves 9.3x / 39.5x; dense line chart 5.5x / 20.4x; SVG to PNG 4.9x / 12.8x; SVG to PDF 5.6x / 17.0x; scale/rotate images 6.6x / 33.5x; gradients 7.8x / 16.3x; text 1.7x / 5.7x; PDF to PNG 1.7x / 3.0x; get/put ImageData only 1.3x / 1.6x; cold start 7 ms vs 108 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Node 24.6.0; prebuilt npm packages skia-canvas v4.0.0-rc6 and canvas v3.2.3 (also @napi-rs/canvas v1.0.10, canvaskit-wasm v0.42.0); native build flags not stated on the results page; run with `npm install && npm run bench` from the benchmark repo
hardware: MacBook Air 13-inch (M3, 2024, Mac15,12): Apple M3 2.4 GHz 8 cores, 24 GiB RAM, macOS 15.7.5
tradeoffs: Node.js native addon only (also runs in Bun/Deno-style hosts via Node-API); depends on Google Skia built into the addon; adds multi-threaded async rendering, PDF/SVG vector export, and Display P3 colour beyond the browser Canvas API; output PNG sizes differ from node-canvas because it picks adaptive PNG filters.
caveats: Benchmarks were run and published by the skia-canvas author (first-party), with the Cairo-based canvas package as baseline. The 'async' rows start every iteration at once inside Promise.all so they measure multi-threading as well as raster speed, whereas the baseline runs one render at a time; the serial rows are the fairer single-render comparison. The gain mostly reflects Skia versus Cairo rather than a new rasterizer. Image get/put is only 1.3x/1.6x. Tier A is generous: the toolchain is prebuilt npm binaries, so compiler and flags are not stated, but versions, CPU and test code are public. In the SVG to SVG and SVG to PDF tests the canvas and @napi-rs/canvas baselines rasterize the SVG to a bitmap while skia-canvas emits vector output, so those rows are not the same work. The tested skia-canvas version is a 4.0.0 release candidate (repo head is already rc8).
found_via: GitHub: README Benchmarks section of samizdatco/skia-canvas, followed to samizdatco/canvas-benchmarks results/darwin-arm64/2026-10-01/index.md (raw.githubusercontent.com), while checking JavaScript canvas libraries for the any-language pass

name: Anti-Grain Geometry (AGG 2.6)

workload: Blend2D-style bl_bench suite: filled and stroked rects, rounded rects, triangles, polygons, butterfly/fish/dragon/world paths with solid, linear and radial fills, SrcOver, 512x600 prgb32 target, shape sizes 8x8 to 256x256, render calls per millisecond, single thread (AGG has no conic or pattern styles in the data: 87 of 174 test rows).
claimed_speedup: Apple M1 Pro, 2026-06-08 run, geometric mean over all test/size cells (derived from page data): 1.21x Skia (faster in 66% of 522 cells; strokes 1.39x, fills 1.08x; only 1.03x at 8x8 and 1.02x at 16x16, 1.39x at 64x64) and 2.29x Cairo (faster in 94% of cells). Intel i9-14900K Windows run (no Skia there): 1.87x Cairo (derived from page data). Slower than Blend2D (0.30x on M1 Pro, derived).
compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release per the harness README; compiler and flags not stated in the result data
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (aarch64, macOS); second dataset Intel Core i9-14900K (x86_64, Windows)
stars_or_usage: 367 stars (GitHub mirror of the SourceForge project)

caveats: Win is workload dependent: against Skia AGG is roughly at parity for tiny shapes (8x8, 16x16) and loses on large rect fills; against Cairo it wins in nearly all cells. The ghaerr repo README notes the bundled General Polygon Clipper code has separate non-commercial terms, so do not copy that part. Last commit on this mirror is 2023-08-21 (a mirror of the SourceForge project, little recent development). The mirror may differ slightly from the AGG copy bundled in blend2d-apps/3rdparty/agg. Ratios are my own aggregation of the published rcpms (render calls per ms) values.

baseline: Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo; also AGG, JUCE, Qt6, CoreGraphics

The runner is the author of Vello CPU (a competitor), and the harness comes from the Blend2D author; the Skia version is not recorded in the data file. name: LunaSVG
baseline: cairosvg 2.9.1 (Python, renders through Cairo 1.18.4) and resvg-py 0.5.0
workload: Median time per icon, SVG bytes to PNG bytes, for 3,460 simple-icons SVGs (24x24 viewBox) scaled to 256 px and 1024 px, plus 943 resvg feature-test SVGs (filters and text excluded), through the pillow-lunasvg Python binding of LunaSVG 3.5.0.
claimed_speedup: simple-icons at 256 px: 1.00 ms vs cairosvg 2.17 ms (2.2x) and resvg-py 2.84 ms (2.8x); at 1024 px: 12.56 ms vs cairosvg 23.63 ms (1.9x) and resvg-py 34.85 ms (2.8x); render-only without PNG encode 0.11 ms at 256 px and 0.88 ms at 1024 px; resvg tests at 1024 px: 5.26 ms vs 19.16 ms cairosvg and 27.22 ms resvg-py.

hardware: Apple M4, macOS 26.5.1

No filters, no SVG inside <image>, no WebP images, no CSS transform property, no transform-origin, no mix-blend-mode, no context-fill. Only 59% of resvg's feature tests match resvg output at 1% pixel tolerance (cairosvg 53%).

This is an SVG-to-PNG pipeline benchmark rather than a pure rasterizer comparison; closest listed baseline relation is Cairo via cairosvg. Benchmark repo has 0 stars; compiler flags not stated, so B rather than A.

name: Vello CPU (sparse strips renderer)
baseline: Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo; also Rust tiny-skia, raqote, AGG, JUCE
workload: Time for 1000 render calls of a single shape (rectangles, many-segment polygons, curves, strokes; solid/gradient/image paints) at sizes 8x8 to 256x256 on a 512x600 pixmap, single-threaded and 8-thread, in a fork of the Blend2D benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: Thesis: Vello CPU 'outperforms nearly all other renderers, including Skia or Cairo, as the shape size increases'; Blend2D still wins in the vast majority of cases. Fill-Solid-RectU 256x256 single-threaded: Vello CPU 14.2 ms vs Skia 50.3 ms (about 3.5x faster, derived from page data) and Cairo 21.9 ms (about 1.5x faster, derived from page data) per 1000 renders; Blend2D 10.8 ms. At small sizes (8x8, 16x16) Skia, AGG and JUCE are faster in some tests. Multi-threaded 8T mode adds speedups up to about 4x on large shapes.
compiler_and_flags: Rust crates built with target-feature=+avx2 on x86 (no extra flags on ARM); build flags of the C++ baselines (Skia, Cairo, Blend2D) not stated in the thesis
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (8 cores, 16 GB) thesis results; Intel Core i9-14900K also run, per vello_chart manifest.json
tradeoffs: Rust crate (vello_cpu); C bindings exist in a separate repo (LaurenzV/vello_cpu_c) so C++ use needs FFI. Weak for very small shapes because of the fixed 4x4 tile size. Supports multi-threading and NEON/AVX2 SIMD.
caveats: Evidence is an ETH Zurich master's thesis (PDF checked into LaurenzV/master-thesis, read via raw.githubusercontent.com) by the Vello CPU author, so the benchmark is first-party for Vello CPU even though the harness is a fork of Blend2D's. Blend2D is faster in nearly all tests, so this is not a win over the category's best. Thesis reports M1 Pro only; interactive results for M1 Pro and i9-14900K live at laurenzv.github.io/vello_chart (blocked here, not opened; repo manifest.json read). The Vello repo README itself has no numbers. Thesis is not formally peer reviewed beyond the university examination, hence B.
found_via: WebSearch: 'sparse strips CPU GPU 2D vector graphics rendering Vello thesis benchmark Skia Blend2D'; then github.com/LaurenzV/master-thesis main.pdf

name: AGG.rs (agg-rust, Rust port of AGG 2.6)
baseline: AGG 2.6 (original C++ library, built with MSVC 19.44)
workload: Render-call time of 11 AGG demo scenes (simple_line, lion_outline, rasterizers2, conv_dash_marker, perspective, image_perspective, image_transforms, image_filters, compositing2, flash_rasterizer, flash_rasterizer2) at 430x340 to 655x520, same scene and size on both sides, output byte-identical to C++; 4 passes x 25 timed iterations after 2 warmups, best-of and median reported.

Medians: 0.56x simple_line to 1.26x rasterizers2.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.91.0 (cargo build --release) versus MSVC 19.44.35219.0 (CMake --config Release); explicit optimisation flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-7660U @ 2.50GHz, Windows 10 (19045)

Project's own benchmark, partial flag information, so tier C.

language: Rust (Node.js and WebAssembly binding of resvg)
baseline: svg2img (canvg plus node-canvas, which is Cairo-based) and sharp (libvips with librsvg)
workload: README 'Sample Benchmark', the 'resize width' suite run with benny: render an SVG to PNG at a different width.
claimed_speedup: resvg-js (Rust) 12 ops/s; sharp 9 ops/s; skr-canvas (Rust) 7 ops/s; svg2img (canvg and node-canvas) 6 ops/s. About 2x svg2img and 1.3x sharp (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: npm i benny@3.x sharp@0.x svg2img@0.x then npm run bench; Node version and build flags not stated
tradeoffs: SVG renderer (resvg on tiny-skia) rather than a general 2D drawing API; Node-API addon plus pure WASM backend that is slower; MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft.
caveats: Weak evidence: README gives integer ops/s for a single SVG and resize with no hardware, Node version or SVG named. The baselines are wrapped Cairo (via node-canvas) and librsvg (via sharp), not Cairo called directly, so baseline_in_list is false. It is an SVG-to-PNG pipeline benchmark, not a pure rasterizer test, and it is a Node binding of the resvg crate (the underlying tiny-skia is already catalogued), so it may fold into a duplicate decision.
found_via: GitHub: README Sample Benchmark section of resvg-js (raw.githubusercontent.com), found while checking resvg descendants for the any-language pass

name: Rive Renderer (rive-runtime)
baseline: Skia (and Flutter Impeller) rendering Rive content
workload: Animated vector tiles drawn on an iPhone 12 (many path-heavy tiles per frame), Rive Renderer vs Skia/Impeller.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: 66x faster, 6000 tiles/sec vs 90 tiles/sec; in one test Skia rendered 9 tiles at about 100 ms (10 fps) while the Rive Renderer rendered 100 tiles at about 16 ms (60 fps).
hardware: iPhone 12 (per snippet)
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars; the renderer behind Rive runtimes
tradeoffs: GPU renderer (Metal, Vulkan, D3D12, D3D11, OpenGL/WebGL, per the README) built around a geometric reduction of anti-aliased paths into triangle patches and best with pixel local storage support; not a CPU rasterizer. Designed for Rive content and its runtime, with an abstract renderer interface (a Skia integration layer and a CoreGraphics renderer also exist in the repo).
caveats: Vendor claim from Rive's own marketing: numbers came from WebSearch snippets of a LinkedIn post by a Rive employee and Rive's blog (rive.app, blocked here and not opened). The repo README makes no performance claim and publishes no numbers; it only mentions a bench binary (out/<config>/bench). A 66x ratio on a hand-picked many-tile animation scenario is over the 50x plausibility line, so it is capped at C. The search snippet itself says benchmarking is difficult and depends heavily on hardware pixel local storage support. No compiler or flags stated.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rive renderer C++ GPU vector rendering faster than Skia benchmark rive-runtime'; github.com/rive-app/rive-runtime opened
WebSearch: 'Rive renderer vs Skia performance benchmark rive-runtime path rendering faster'

name: stilus
baseline: golang.org/x/image/vector (the Go project's rasterizer) and gogpu/gg v0.52.5 CPU rasterizer
workload: Synthetic print-style scenes on an A3 landscape page at 150 dpi (2481x1754 px): 2,000 hatch lines and 20,000 short strokes. stilus strokes and fills directly; the x/image/vector run fills the outlines produced by stilus's own stroker, with one vector.Rasterizer sized to each outline's bounding box; gg runs with no clip.
claimed_speedup: README comparison table: 2 000 hatch lines: stilus 70 ms, x/image/vector 33 400 ms, gogpu/gg 14 800 ms; 20 000 short strokes: stilus 55 ms, x/image/vector 111 ms, gogpu/gg 2 090 ms. About 477x and 2.0x versus x/image/vector (derived from page data). Separate 'Numbers' table: stilus 1 core 67 ms (2 000 hatch lines at 0.35 mm) and 41 ms (20 000 short strokes), 4 cores 19 ms and 12 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Go (go.mod says go 1.24; toolchain version for the table not stated); `cd bench && go test -bench .`, comparison source is bench/compare_test.go (separate module)
hardware: 'Same machine' as the Numbers table: cloud Xeon @ 2.1 GHz (exact model not stated), minimum of 15 runs; some speed levers were measured on a Ryzen 7 5800H
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no cgo, no dependencies, builds for all GOOS/GOARCH including js/wasm; zero allocations after warm-up; sparse cost model (edge length plus covered spans); exact-area coverage like FreeType/AGG; optional AVX2/AVX-512 compositing under GOEXPERIMENT=simd; it is only the rasterizer core of a planned PDF renderer (no fonts, colour spaces or display lists).
caveats: The baseline is used in a way that favours stilus: x/image/vector's cost is proportional to the bounding-box area, so long diagonal hatch lines cost it a full box each, which explains the 477x ratio (above 50x, so capped at tier C). It is not compared against Skia, Cairo or Blend2D, so baseline_in_list is false; the README only checks quality against PDFium (mean deviation 0.3-1.5/255, SSIM at least 0.998). First-party, one author, synthetic scenes, CPU model not named exactly, Go toolchain version not stated for the comparison table; benchmark source was skimmed, not run.
found_via: GitHub: topic page github.com/topics/rasterizer?l=go and vector-graphics?l=go, then README Numbers and comparison tables of timzifer/stilus and bench/compare_test.go via raw.githubusercontent.com

The separate tdewolff/canvas_benchmarks repo compares polygon boolean operations (Clipper, Clipper2, iOverlay), not rasterization. First-party, no stated methodology, one extreme case.

name: TFT_eSPI
baseline: Adafruit_GFX (Adafruit-GFX-Library)
workload: Arduino_GFX README 'Performance' table: per-primitive drawing benchmark (screen fill, text, pixels, lines, horizontal/vertical lines, rectangles, triangles, circles, arcs, rounded rectangles; filled and outline variants) pushed to an ILI9341 over SPI, comparing Adafruit_GFX, Arduino_GFX, LovyanGFX and TFT_eSPI.
claimed_speedup: README table of the Arduino_GFX repository, TFT_eSPI versus Adafruit_GFX (units not stated, lower is faster): Text 21,752 vs 97,662 (4.5x); Lines 264,950 vs 1,062,311 (4.0x); Circles 25,269 vs 118,125 (4.7x); Triangles 16,277 vs 58,843 (3.6x); Screen fill 155,938 vs 195,782 (1.3x); Rectangles-filled 323,908 vs 406,817; ratios derived from page data. The TFT_eSPI README itself says the library is 'performance optimised' for RP2040, STM32, ESP8266 and ESP32 but gives no comparison numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Arduino IDE 1.8.15 with the arduino-esp32 1.0.6 default toolchain; compiler flags not stated
hardware: TTGO T8 v1.8 (ESP32) board, PSRAM disabled, ILI9341 display on SPI at 40 MHz; Arduino IDE 1.8.15, arduino-esp32 1.0.6; test date 2021-06-16 (exact ESP32 CPU clock not stated)
stars_or_usage: 4.9k stars; widely used Arduino and PlatformIO TFT library
tradeoffs: Grew out of Adafruit_ILI9341 and Adafruit_GFX; DMA on ESP32, RP2040 and STM32, 8 and 16-bit parallel interfaces, sprites for flicker-free updates, smooth anti-aliased arcs, circles and rounded rectangles, anti-aliased TrueType via the OpenFontRender add-on; user-setup header files select the display and processor; generic processors fall back to slow Arduino SPI calls.
caveats: Table is published in the README of Arduino_GFX, a competing library whose own README says 'This library is not putting speed at the first priority'; units of the numbers are not stated; benchmark code is not linked from the table (the README only recommends the PDQgraphicstest example); no library versions, compiler flags or run counts; dated 2021-06-16 so current versions may differ; the test is bound by the SPI link and the display controller, so it measures driver and primitive-routine overhead on a microcontroller, not raster throughput comparable to Skia, Cairo or Blend2D; a display driver stack with primitives, not a general path rasterizer. The numbers were measured by the author of a competing library, not by the TFT_eSPI project. The most recent commits (2026-02 to 2026-04) are README and board-header updates, and the repository shows many open issues and pull requests. license.txt combines the FreeBSD two-clause licence for the original code with the Adafruit BSD and MIT notices of the code it started from; the bundled fonts have separate licence files.
found_via: WebSearch: 'LovyanGFX OR TFT_eSPI benchmark faster than Adafruit_GFX fill rect text drawing speed comparison'; Arduino_GFX README Performance table

name: TGFX (Tencent Graphics)
baseline: Skia (m136)
workload: TGFX Benchmark rectangle test: number of rectangles each engine can draw while holding 60 FPS (basic Rect rendering only).
claimed_speedup: '510,308 Rectangles at 60 FPS' for TGFX versus '34,721 Rectangles at 60 FPS' for Skia; announcement text: 'renders rectangles at least 10 times faster than Skia's m136 version - reaching up to 16 times faster' and 'Basic graphics (such as Rect) rendering is 10x faster compared to version 1.2' (ratio of the two counts is about 14.7x, derived from page data).
