name: ThorVG
baseline: Skia (CPU raster backend, Skia v148)
workload: Frames per second drawing 5,000 semi-transparent primitives (rects, rotated rects, strokes, circles, PNG images, gradients) with alpha blending at 2560x1440 on the CPU backend, ThorVG v1.1 vs Skia v148, using the thorvg.benchmark app.
claimed_speedup: README: average ~2.9x faster than Skia on CPU. Per-case fps from the README chart image (ThorVG vs Skia): Rects 76.0 vs 17.2 (4.4x); Rotated Rects 36.0 vs 10.1 (3.6x); Stroke 55.7 vs 17.2 (3.2x); Rects+Stroke 41.8 vs 10.5 (4.0x); Rotated Rects+Stroke 25.0 vs 4.5 (5.6x); Circles 38.5 vs 10.4 (3.7x); Images (PNG) 6.4 vs 6.0 (1.1x); Rotated Images 4.4 vs 4.4 (1.0x); Linear Gradient 9.0 vs 8.5 (1.1x); Radial Gradient 6.9 vs 6.0 (1.2x).
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark harness built with CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; ThorVG built with meson -Dloaders=all -Dengines=all; Skia installed through vcpkg (config not stated); compiler version not stated
hardware: Apple M2 Pro, macOS 26
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; used by Canva (Lottie), SEGGER, Lottie Creator per README
tradeoffs: Smaller feature set than Skia (core binary about 170KB per README); focused on SVG and Lottie, with software, OpenGL and WebGPU backends. Per the VGCPU-Benchmark README its CPU rasterizer uses a sum-then-saturate coverage model (not exact union), so self-overlapping paths can differ from Skia and Cairo. The gain is large for rect, stroke and circle workloads but only 1.0x to 1.2x for images and gradients.
caveats: First-party benchmark from the ThorVG maintainers. The per-case numbers were read from the chart image (thorvg.site repo, readme/example_performance.png, fetched through raw.githubusercontent.com) that the README displays; the README text itself states only the ~2.9x average and the test conditions. The benchmark code is public (github.com/thorvg/thorvg.benchmark, opened, MIT) but compiler and flags are not stated, so this is C, not A. Skia comes from a vcpkg build with unknown options; Skia CPU raster is single-threaded while ThorVG has an optional task-scheduler thread pool and the benchmark setup installs libomp, thread counts are not stated. The maintainers' own discussion (github.com/orgs/thorvg/discussions/1815, opened) quotes outside criticism that Blend2D beats ThorVG's software renderer significantly and says no formal Blend2D comparison existed at that time, so there is no evidence ThorVG beats Blend2D.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/2d-graphics?l=c%2B%2B; github.com/topics/vector-graphics?l=c%2B%2B; WebSearch 'SVG renderer speed comparison benchmark lunasvg plutosvg thorvg resvg'
WebSearch: '"vector graphics" rasterizer C++ "faster than Blend2D" OR "faster than Skia" CPU SIMD paper github 2025' surfaced thorvg PR 4849; README and thorvg.benchmark opened

name: tiny-skia
baseline: Cairo (and raqote); slower than Skia
workload: CPU 2D rendering of common operations (fills, strokes, gradients, patterns, clipping) in the project's benchmark set.
claimed_speedup: README: 20-100% slower than Skia on x86-64 and about 100-300% slower on ARM, 'which is still faster than cairo and raqote in many cases'.
tradeoffs: A minimal Skia subset ported to Rust (about 14k lines, about 200KB, no text, no GPU); not a Skia replacement. Needs FFI from C++.
caveats: The win over Cairo is stated only as 'in many cases' and the detailed results page (linebender.github.io/tiny-skia/x86_64.html) is blocked. It loses to Skia, so the claim is relative to Cairo only. In the Vello CPU thesis, tiny-skia is slower than Vello CPU and Skia in the shown tests, so the Cairo advantage may not hold across workloads (e.g. Fill-Solid-RectA 256x256: tiny-skia 136 ms vs Cairo 18.6 ms). Rust-only.
found_via: Read README after the Vello CPU thesis named tiny-skia as a compared Rust renderer

name: tiny-skia-cpp
baseline: Rust tiny-skia (linebender/tiny-skia, a Skia subset)
workload: 512x512 FillRect and FillPath rendering, C++ SIMD backend vs the Rust tiny-skia implementation, normalized to Rust = 1.0x (ARM measured on Apple Silicon NEON, x86 on Intel/AMD with AVX2+FMA).
claimed_speedup: Up to 1.9x faster than Rust tiny-skia: FillRect ARM 1.9x, x86 1.3x; FillPath ARM 1.4x, x86 1.2x; SIMD speedup over the C++ scalar backend up to 2.3x (x86 AVX2) and 1.9x (ARM NEON).
hardware: Apple Silicon (NEON) and Intel/AMD (AVX2+FMA), exact CPU models not stated
tradeoffs: CPU-only C++20 port of the Skia-subset algorithms with x86-64 AVX2+FMA and ARM64 NEON backends plus a scalar fallback, zero dependencies, Bazel or CMake. Output is near-pixel-accurate against Rust tiny-skia, not bit-exact (extra analytic AA and filter primitives). Only a subset of Skia features.
caveats: The baseline is the Rust port, not Skia, Cairo or Blend2D, so this does not show it beats those. A WebSearch snippet of the Rust tiny-skia docs (not opened) says tiny-skia is 20-100% slower than Skia on x86-64 and 100-300% slower on ARM, which means the C++ port is likely still not faster than Skia itself. Only two workloads at one size, CPU models and compiler flags not stated; the repo has benchmark code (tests/benchmarks with RenderPerfBench.cpp and run_render_perf_compare.sh, which compare C++ SIMD, C++ scalar and Rust via FFI) so the claim is reproducible but missing methodology. Repo is small and recent with a bot commit as the latest.
found_via: WebSearch: 'faster than Blend2D OR faster than Skia CPU vector graphics rasterizer C++ library github'

name: vger (Audulus)
language: C (C API over Metal; distributed as a Swift package)
baseline: nanovg
workload: Rendering the Audulus immediate-mode UI on a 120Hz iPad; frame rate with vger versus with nanovg.
claimed_speedup: 'vger maintains 120fps while nanovg falls to 30fps on my 120Hz iPad because of CPU-side path tessellation, and other overhead' (4x frame rate, derived from page data).
hardware: 120Hz iPad (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Apple platforms only (iOS and macOS, Metal); limited primitive set drawn as instanced quads with analytic fragment-shader evaluation (quadratic Bezier strokes, round rectangles, circles, arcs, text, path fills); C interface usable from C, C++, Objective-C and Swift, but vgerEncode must be called from Objective-C or Swift because it takes an MTLCommandBuffer; non-Apple users are pointed to the Rust port vger-rs.
caveats: Single anecdotal first-party figure from the README 'Why?' section for one app and one iPad; no benchmark code, no nanovg version, no scene description and no frame-time numbers; baseline nanovg is not Skia, Cairo or Blend2D, and the README attributes nanovg's slowdown to CPU-side path tessellation in this app's workload; not a CPU rasterizer.
found_via: github.com/topics/vector-graphics?l=c and github.com/topics/2d-graphics?l=c (audulus/vger), README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: vkvg
baseline: Cairo (GL ES3 backend) and Skia (Vulkan backend)
workload: vgperf, a caskbench-style C harness, drawing lines/strokes, rectangles, circles and stars with vkvg (Vulkan), Cairo (GL es3) and Skia (Vulkan).
claimed_speedup: Chart only (y-axis has no label or unit, probably time per frame where lower is better); approximate bar values read from the chart image (derived from page data): lines stroke vkvg ~0.00013, cairo es3 ~0.0031, skia ~0.0004; rectangles ~0.00025, ~0.00025, ~0.0002; circles vkvg ~0.00065, cairo ~0.0035, skia ~0.00016; stars vkvg ~0.00058, cairo ~0.0019, skia ~0.00062. So vkvg beats Cairo es3 on 3 of 4 tests and ties on rectangles; it beats Skia only on lines stroke and loses clearly on circles.
compiler_and_flags: Skia built with gn args is_official_build=true is_component_build=true skia_use_vulkan=true (vgperf README); vkvg and Cairo flags not stated
tradeoffs: Needs Vulkan; GPU-only; Cairo-like C API; alpha-stage per README; fill (stencil even-odd and non-zero), stroke, gradients, dashes and a font system with caching are implemented.
caveats: First-party chart with no axis label, unit, GPU or CPU model, run count or Cairo/vkvg versions, so the numbers are approximate readings of a PNG and the metric direction is inferred. vgperf (5 stars, 22 commits, MIT) has no numeric results, only the chart; Skia was built from a patched experimental C API branch. Only 4 simple drawing tests. Mixed result against Skia. Cairo is measured through its GL ES3 backend, not its image (CPU) backend.

name: gopus (pure-Go Opus codec)
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (C reference encoder and decoder, SIMD build)
workload: Matched C and Go encode and decode workloads in ns per sample per channel: CELT fullband 20 ms stereo 128 kbps, CELT 5 ms mono 64 kbps, SILK wideband 20 ms mono 32 kbps, Hybrid fullband mono 64 kbps and stereo 96 kbps encode; decode of 20,075 RFC test-vector packets as float32 and int16.
claimed_speedup: Go SIMD takes 2.5-28.7% less time than matched C SIMD in four of five encoder cases (for example SILK wideband 329.21 vs 462.01 ns/sample, Hybrid fullband mono 225.80 vs 253.40, CELT fullband 20 ms stereo 126.28 vs 129.50) and 14.6% more in the 5 ms CELT case; float32 decode 33.14 vs 35.90 (7.7% less), int16 decode 37.64 vs 38.83 (3.1% less). Scalar rows: Go scalar is slower than C scalar in 6 of 7 rows (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.1 with GOAMD64=v3, GOEXPERIMENT=simd and PGO; C side GCC 13.3.0 with GOPUS_LIBOPUS_AMD64_TARGET=v3 (same x86-64-v3 target); each case three runs of at least 250 ms; reproduce with tools/encoderbenchcmp and tools/testvectorbenchcmp
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763
tradeoffs: Go-only (no cgo) so C++ use needs an FFI shim or a Go service; the win needs GOAMD64=v3 and GOEXPERIMENT=simd, a Go 1.27 toolchain feature, and PGO; the README says the Go build tracks libopus 1.6.1 for bit-exact and quality parity, with optional DRED, QEXT and OSCE builds behind build tags.
caveats: First-party harness, but the comparison tools are public and the revision (candidate 4b660d668) and toolchains are named. Results are a mix: Go is slower in the scalar table and in one SIMD encoder case, and the faster rows are 3-29% rather than multiples. Measures codec work only, not file I/O. The README states its own file-based bench-encode and bench-decode examples include opus_demo process start-up in the C timings and are only rough. The repo shows 3,296 commits; the benchmarks were not run by this agent. The fork hujm2023/gopus (0 stars) shows older CI numbers where Go is 1.3-1.7x slower than libopus; those were not used.
found_via: WebSearch: 'pure Go Opus OR FLAC OR MP3 decoder faster than libopus OR libFLAC cgo benchmark github'; then opened thesyncim/gopus README (Performance section) and commits page

name: libopus-rs
baseline: libopus (Opus trunk commit 03647f524a40b05a1898522e92033810b58103c7)
workload: 48 kHz stereo CELT-only, 5 ms (240-sample) frames, maximum complexity, 16-bit and 24-bit PCM, CBR and constrained VBR at 192/256/320 kb/s; direct in-process encode and decode of 4 x 10 s excerpts, three alternating Rust/C rounds, median per source.
claimed_speedup: Encode 1.19-2.36% less time and decode 1.50-4.64% less time than trunk libopus in all 12 aggregate cells (e.g. 16-bit CBR 192 kb/s: encode 371.9 ms vs 380.9 ms, decode 95.3 ms vs 100.0 ms per 40 s of audio); Rust encoder 96.8-107.6x realtime, decoder 338-430x realtime.
compiler_and_flags: Rust release mode, ThinLTO, one codegen unit, -C target-cpu=native; C driver (tools/raw_celt_bench.c) built with -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native and linked against static libopus.a from the trunk commit; the final timing JSON records the build-flag fields as unknown because binaries were reused; compiler versions not stated.
hardware: GCP c4-highcpu-4, Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C, process pinned to CPU 2 with taskset
tradeoffs: Incomplete codec: only 48 kHz CELT-only raw frames are supported; no SILK, hybrid or Ogg Opus. Not a drop-in replacement for libopus, no C API, and encoder packets are not byte-identical to libopus. Encoder is marked experimental. Uses a private SIMD kernel path dependency crate.
caveats: Gain is only a few percent and measured on a narrow configuration (5 ms CELT, max complexity). The test corpus (SoundKit diverse-v1) is licensed local audio and is not stored in the repo, so the run is not reproducible as-is. The repository is archived and deprecated in favour of wavey-ai/soundkit (soundkit-opus/libopus-rs) per its README; that successor was not opened. Quality was checked by SNR and ViSQOL, not listening tests.
found_via: crates.io API searches (libopus, pure rust codec, and others) then a raw README scan of audio/video crate repos; opened github.com/wavey-ai/libopus-rs, its commits page, tools folder and the 2026-08-24 performance report

name: opus-pure
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (float build)
workload: Opus encode and decode of generated 48 kHz speech/music test signals, 20 ms frames, complexity 9, in-process, 8 s of audio per case, fastest of 12 passes, run through SILK, hybrid and CELT modes.
claimed_speedup: Encode 1.09-1.76x faster than libopus (SILK 1.09-1.12x, e.g. 218x vs 195x realtime for SILK NB 8 kb/s mono; CELT 128 kb/s 204x vs 116x realtime = 1.76x); decode slower or at parity, 0.84-1.02x of libopus (e.g. SILK NB 3432x vs 3958x realtime).
compiler_and_flags: Rust crate at cargo default release settings, no RUSTFLAGS, no -march=native (rustc version only stated as 1.88 or newer); libopus 1.6.1 built with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, OPUS_USE_NEON=ON with runtime dispatch, float build (also a fixed-point build for a second column); C compiler not named.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (aarch64 NEON)
stars_or_usage: 2 stars; 19+ commits; on crates.io as opus-pure
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no C API or FFI exposed (callable from C++ only by writing a wrapper); no dependencies; hand-written NEON/SIMD kernels for CELT. Decode is not faster than libopus. Chunk-parallel encode is lossy relative to serial encode. Ogg reader seeks only to the start.
caveats: Single machine (aarch64 Apple M1 Pro); x86 results are not given. SILK encode is a fixed-point port, so the harness reports a second table against fixed-point libopus where the ratio differs. The README states hybrid is not exactly like-for-like with either libopus build. The harness (cspeed.c, rspeed, run.sh) is in the repo, which is why this is tier A; the toolchain versions are not pinned.
found_via: crates.io API searches (opus, audio codec, libopus, and others) then a raw README scan of about 1,500 audio/video crate repos for speed claims against named baselines; opened github.com/stephenberry/opus-pure, its commits page and reference/speed

name: opuspp
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 decoder (opus_decode_float), built with identical compiler and flags
workload: Decoding a 60 s mixed-audio stream (tones, noise, transients, orchestral music) encoded by libopus as 48 kHz fullband stereo, 10 ms CELT frames at 320 kb/s and encoder complexity 4; best of 7 passes pinned to one core, packet buffer flushed from cache before each pass. Other streams: 128 and 510 kb/s, 10% packet loss, complexity 0 and 2.
claimed_speedup: Like for like (same compiler and flags) opuspp is 1.27x to 1.48x faster than libopus at 320 kb/s (GCC Size 1.27x, GCC Balanced 1.48x, GCC Fast 1.43x, Clang Size 1.42x, Clang Balanced 1.46x, Clang Fast 1.42x); 1.09x to 1.50x across other bit rates, packet loss and encoder complexities. Five of six opuspp builds beat the fastest libopus build (GCC Fast) by 1.33x to 1.43x; GCC Size opuspp is slower than that build (0.88x).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.2 and Clang 22.1; Size: -Os, Balanced: -O2, Fast: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -falign-loops=32 (libopus with OPUS_FLOAT_APPROX=ON and OPUS_FAST_MATH=ON, opuspp with OPUSPP_FLOAT_APPROX); all with -DNDEBUG -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections and -Wl,--gc-sections
hardware: One core of an AMD Ryzen 5 9600X

Against upstream rav1d with assembly the same page set shows checked rav1d-safe taking 1.8-8.6 times as long, and its README reports about 1.5x slower than the assembly build on 4K and 8K AVIF stills.

name: Falcon audio codec
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (float and fixed point), opusfile 0.12, libvorbis 1.3.7, Tremor (decoders)
workload: Library-level single-thread decode of an 18-file 48 kHz stereo corpus (11 real recordings plus 7 synthetic signals) from memory to PCM in 20 ms reads, with Falcon and Opus files at equal size and Vorbis at its own quality setting; total times real time over the corpus, plus 256 simultaneous stereo voices.
claimed_speedup: Falcon 1114x real time vs libopus 1.6.1 float 731x (Falcon time 0.66x of libopus), libopus fixed point 629x, opusfile 717x, libvorbis 879x (0.79x), Tremor 877x (0.79x) on an x86-64 laptop performance core; Apple M5 1551x vs libopus float 1056x (0.68x) and libvorbis 1297x (0.84x). Faster than libopus on 18 of 18 files on both CPUs; stb_vorbis 1154x is on par on x86-64 and 1.28x faster on M5. 256 voices: 291 ms vs libopus float 365 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Falcon: Rust release profile, fat LTO, one codegen unit, x86-64-v3 on x86-64 (MSVC-toolchain DLL on Windows); C decoders built with -O3, GCC 15.1 (MinGW-w64) -march=x86-64-v3 on x86-64 and Apple clang 17 on M5; libopus with default SSE4.1/AVX2 runtime dispatch, stack protector off; best of two passes, at least 10 runs and 1 s per file
hardware: Intel Core Ultra 9 185H laptop (Windows 11, thread pinned to one performance, efficiency or low-power efficiency core) and a MacBook Pro with Apple M5 (macOS 26)
tradeoffs: A different codec, not a drop-in decoder for Opus streams: Falcon is an MDCT codec whose decoder is deliberately light and whose quality comes from encoder-side work. Uses more memory per stream than libopus (about 320-345 KB of heap per stereo stream plus a copy of the compressed file, vs 27 KB for libopus) and voice start-up is slower (156 us vs 46 us). Includes a C/C++ API (falcon_capi) with falcon.h and falcon.hpp. Quality claim is on par with Opus on an 18-file corpus, not an independent listening test. Version 2 was redesigned to avoid specific patents.
caveats: First-party numbers on one laptop CPU and one Apple CPU. The C comparison program that links all decoders was not found in the repo (tools/ holds only eval and quality; falcon_capi/examples hold decode examples), so the table cannot be reproduced from the repo as far as opened. The README says earlier versions compared against FFmpeg's built-in Opus and Vorbis decoders by mistake and withdrew the old Vorbis figures; against FFmpeg's Vorbis decoder Falcon wins only 5 of 18 files. Raw libopus is fed pre-extracted packets (no Ogg parsing) while opusfile, vorbisfile and stb_vorbis include container parsing. Falcon is Opus-class quality at equal size per its own metrics, but speed compares a different codec at the same file size, not the same bitstream.

claimed_speedup: Snippet only: 'QOA encodes 10x faster and decodes 7x faster than Opus'; '25.75 seconds to encode a 9807-second file, 5.7 times faster than MP3 encoding on an i7-6700k'; decoding faster than Opus on an i7-6700k single-threaded. The repo README and qoa.h contain no benchmark, so the verifier needs the blog post or a rerun. Compiler, flags and files are unknown. name: remade_ffmpeg_rs
baseline: FFmpeg libavcodec native MP3 decoder and native AAC encoder; libvorbis
workload: MP3 decode of a 27.5-minute stream, decode-and-discard on the same physical cores, 15 pairs; AAC-LC encode of a 60 s stereo clip with frame-parallel encoding; Vorbis encode of stereo music on 24 cores.
claimed_speedup: MP3 decode 1.24x faster than FFmpeg on 1 core (1,952 vs 2,431 ms, 15/15 pairs) and 1.39x on 2 cores (1,017 vs 1,455 ms), at lower total CPU (1,875 vs 2,125 ms); AAC encode about 6x faster than ffmpeg's own AAC encoder via frame-parallel encoding (about 450x realtime; single-thread about 1.15x); Vorbis encode about 5.3x faster than libvorbis wall-clock (frame-parallel, 24 cores; per-thread about 1.4x behind libvorbis). Image side (not video-audio): PNG decode 2.55-2.89x faster than ffmpeg, lossy WebP decode 1.24-1.29x.

The AAC and Vorbis headline speedups come from multi-threaded frame-parallel encoding against single-threaded baselines. Video codecs are slower than the incumbents: VP9 decode about 0.16-0.21x of FFmpeg, VP9 encode about 0.3x at +36% bit rate, H.264 decode about 2x behind FFmpeg's native decoder, MP3 encoder about 0.7-1.1 ODG behind LAME on average (1.4-1.8 on transients).

The README itself notes an earlier CLI-to-CLI comparison had MP3 decode 1.20x behind and was corrected to a matched-core comparison. The repo carries CLAUDE.md and .claude directories (AI-assisted). The crates rusty_mp3, rusty_aac, rusty_vorbis share this repo URL, so any standalone listing needs a paper: id to avoid duplicates. Only the README text was read; the code was not.

name: ropus (Rust port of libopus)
baseline: libopus 1.5.2 (C reference, with its hand-tuned SSE4.1/AVX2 dispatch)
workload: Encode and decode time ratio Rust over C on ten WAV vectors (SILK narrowband and wideband noise, Hybrid noise, CELT noise, sine, sweep, square, TTS speech, stereo music), harness amortising codec construction, medians of five sweeps (tools/bench_sweep.sh --iters=30).
claimed_speedup: x86-64 ratios Rust/C (below 1.0 means Rust faster): encode SILK NB noise 0.97x, SILK WB noise 0.96x, Hybrid noise 0.97x, CELT sweep 0.96x; decode CELT square 0.92x, SILK NB 0.95x, CELT FB mono noise 0.98x, CELT sine 0.99x; means 1.06x encode and 1.01x decode (slightly slower overall). The README says Rust encode is faster than C on five vectors and decode faster or at parity on six.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler version and C flags not stated in the README; Rust build targets x86-64-v3 (AVX2, FMA3, BMI1/2) per the README CPU-target note; harness is tools/bench_sweep.sh driving the ropus-compare binary
hardware: Intel i7-14700KF under WSL2 (x86-64 table); Apple M1 Pro (second table, where decode is slower, for example SILK NB 1.30x and SILK WB 1.50x); earlier Ryzen 9 9950X3D baseline kept in a journal
license: BSD-3-Clause (the repo LICENSE is the upstream Xiph libopus licence text; the README says to refer to the upstream project licence)
tradeoffs: Rust port of libopus 1.5.2 including DNN features (LPCNet, FARGAN, DRED) with a C ABI shim (capi/) that exposes the libopus API, plus a differential FFI harness that compares byte-for-byte against the C reference; builds the C reference from a pinned xiph/opus checkout. Larger binary because of an embedded 8.78 MB weights blob.
caveats: Parity rather than a win: mean encode ratio is 1.06x (slower) and mean decode 1.01x on x86-64, and decode is 1.3-1.5x slower on some Apple M1 Pro rows. The README says earlier runs measured decoder construction cost, not steady-state decode. Single desktop CPU, compiler flags not given, first-party. The repo carries CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md (AI-assisted). Recorded because a few vectors are faster than the C baseline; the honest summary is roughly equal speed.

name: ruopus
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (SIMD-enabled C)
workload: In-process Opus encode and decode of a generated 6 s mono speech/music-like 48 kHz signal in 20 ms frames, one core, expressed as times realtime (benches/vs_libopus.rs).
claimed_speedup: Decode faster than SIMD libopus on speech: SILK wideband 16 kb/s 2095x vs 1171x realtime (1.79x), hybrid fullband 32 kb/s 1199x vs 850x (1.41x); CELT fullband 64 kb/s 1389x vs 1566x (0.89x, slower). Encode at matched complexity 0 is at parity (0.99-1.00x); against libopus default complexity 10, SILK wideband 16 kb/s encode 703x vs 221x (3.18x).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --bench vs_libopus --features std; release profile opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1 (Cargo.toml); libopus 1.6.1 reached through the opus FFI crate against the system libopus, so its build flags are not stated.
hardware: one core pinned to a single performance core; CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 1 star; on crates.io as ruopus (about 6.9k downloads)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust Opus encoder and decoder with Python bindings and wasm32 support; no C API or FFI exposed, so C++ use needs a wrapper. Encoder does not yet implement delayed-decision noise-shaping quantization or warped noise shaping.
caveats: CPU model and OS not stated. The 3.18x encode figure compares a ruopus encoder with no complexity-dependent slowdown against libopus at complexity 10, so the work is not equal; at matched complexity 0 encode is at parity. CELT decode is slower than libopus. Benchmark signal is synthetic. Benchmark harness is public (benches/vs_libopus.rs) but flags of the linked libopus are unknown.

workload: Single-thread encode of 300 s and 150 s clips driven as processes, reporting the slope t(300 s) minus t(150 s), pinned to one core, CPU time, ABBA-interleaved, 31 reps, with a null arm; split by coding path verified from TOC bytes (CELT 48 kHz speech at 32k, CELT 48 kHz stereo music at 128k, SILK 16 kHz speech at 16k).

name: SampleRateTap (async engine)
baseline: libsamplerate 0.2.2 (Secret Rabbit Code, MEDIUM and BEST converters)
workload: Asynchronous near-unity sample rate conversion (two clock domains) measured as million output frames per second for mono, stereo and 8-channel streams at a matched ~120 dB and ~140 dB stopband tier, plus algorithmic latency and embedded instruction counts.
claimed_speedup: Doc states SampleRateTap is 3.1-3.9x (stereo/mono; 1.5x at 8 channels) faster than libsamplerate at the matched ~120 dB tier and 6.1x at ~140 dB, with 2-3.6x less latency. Table: stereo 14.6 vs 4.8 Mframes/s (balanced vs libsamplerate MEDIUM), mono 20.3 vs 5.2, 8-ch 3.0 vs 1.9; ~140 dB stereo 9.6 vs 1.6 (BEST). The same table shows soxr HQ at 52.9 and r8brain-free-src at 16.5 stereo, i.e. it is SLOWER than soxr and r8brain on x86 host throughput.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3 -O3 (CMake Release); libsamplerate 0.2.2 and soxr 0.1.3 Ubuntu 24.04 packages; r8brain at pinned commit 7.5 with Ooura FFT
hardware: shared Xeon @ 2.10 GHz (exact model not stated), run 2026-09-25; embedded rows use QEMU instruction counting for Cortex-M33 and Hexagon
tradeoffs: Specialised: near-unity asynchronous ratio (+-1000 ppm default) for clock-domain bridging, not a general-ratio resampler. Header-only C++20. Fixed-point Q15/Q31 paths for FPU-less DSPs. Very low latency (0.5 ms filter, 1.5 ms default).
caveats: Only beats libsamplerate; the same page shows soxr HQ (52.9 stereo) and r8brain (16.5 stereo) faster on x86 host throughput, which the author states openly. Measured on a shared Xeon with exact CPU model missing and ratios said to be the meaningful figures; libsamplerate latency rows were measured on 2026-06-12. Benchmark code is in the repo behind TAP_SR_BUILD_COMPARE_BENCH (off by default). Very young repo (commits Sep 30 to Oct 3 2026 visible, 225 commits), 5 stars; the benchmark page was written by the project author (first-party).

name: SuperFast Codecs (fre:ac multi-threaded codec drivers)
baseline: fre:ac's regular single-threaded codec drivers: libopus (Opus), FAAC and Core Audio AAC in the initial release; FDK-AAC, LAME and Speex drivers added later
workload: Converting a single input file to a single output file with 4 worker threads, each running its own codec instance on overlapping 128-frame blocks (8-frame overlap).
claimed_speedup: 'Using four threads, the conversion is already three times faster than with the regular drivers, which use only a single thread in this mode' (single file mode). In multi file mode the SuperFast drivers are only slightly faster. The measured chart is an image in the PDF; the text gives no per-codec table.
hardware: Not stated (the text mentions a 6 core CPU)
stars_or_usage: 65 stars; code merged into mainline fre:ac (BoCA)
tradeoffs: Chunked parallelism over several codec instances, so output is not bit-identical to a single-threaded encode and the 8/128 overlap caps speedup at 16x. Works for Opus, AAC, Speex and MP3 drivers; the author says Vorbis, FLAC and WMA do not fit. Needs the fre:ac BoCA and smooth class libraries to build. It speeds up a driver, not the codec library itself.
caveats: First-party blog post (PDF) whose numbers are only in a chart image; CPU, thread counts per test and codec versions are not given in text, so tier C. The comparison is multi-threaded drivers against the same codec run single-threaded, not a faster codec implementation. Repo is archived since 2020-12-11 (code lives on in enzo1982/BoCA). The Opus resampler in the pipeline stays single-threaded, which limits gains for non-48 kHz input.

name: SuperLAME
baseline: LAME (stock single-threaded libmp3lame 3.101 beta)
workload: Encoding a 44-minute album to CBR 320 kb/s MP3, 2 to 16 threads, in-RAM benchmark mode.
claimed_speedup: 'Roughly 8x faster than stock single-threaded LAME at the same quality'; Ryzen 7 5800X3D, v1.1.0: 13.8 s at 2 threads down to 3.9 s at 16 threads (about 680x realtime); parallel efficiency about 93% at 2 workers and about 61% at 16.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ -std=c++17 -O2 -march=x86-64 for the frontend, clang -O2 for dr_flac, plus four libmp3lame engine builds (znver5, znver4, znver3, SSE2) in one binary; Windows executable
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X3D
tradeoffs: Runs many libmp3lame instances in parallel on chunks and repairs the bit reservoir, so the gain is thread parallelism. Single-thread output is bit-identical to stock LAME; multi-thread output differs by an inaudible (below -45 dB) reconciliation at chunk seams. Whole input and output are held in RAM (about 1-2 GB input limit). Needs clang to build the SIMD paths; GPL because it combines LGPL LAME and mpg123 with GPL code ported from fre:ac/BoCA.
caveats: First-party README numbers; the stock-LAME timing that the 8x is measured against is not shown on the page, and the 8x applies to multi-threaded use on a many-core desktop. A --bench mode and tests/scaling.ps1 are described (not opened or run). Very new repo (July 2026) with 3 stars. Windows-oriented.

Snippet only (Netflix Tech Blog 2020 and third-party guides, pages blocked): similar compression efficiency to libaom with significantly lower encoding latency on multi-core platforms; third-party posts quote 10-50x faster than libaom.
stars_or_usage: 75 stars on the GitHub mirror; canonical repo on GitLab (5,270 commits, 45 releases); founded by Intel with Netflix and adopted by the Alliance for Open Media
tradeoffs: Encoder only. Faster presets give up compression efficiency; at the slowest presets it only reaches similar efficiency to libaom. Licensed BSD-3-Clause-Clear plus the AOM Patent License 1.0.
caveats: The numbers on the opened page are 'similar speed' statements, not a speedup ratio over libaom or x265. The libaom claim comes only from search snippets of blocked pages (snippet only). The README links peer-reviewed SPIE and ICIP papers (SPIE 2020 'The SVT-AV1 encoder: overview, features and speed-quality tradeoffs') that were not opened. Other changelog entries cite speed comparisons only against earlier SVT-AV1 versions on AWS Graviton4 with Clang 19/20.

WebSearch: 'SVT-AV1 paper scalable encoder faster than libaom speed compression efficiency tradeoff'; gitlab.com/AOMediaCodec/SVT-AV1 README and CHANGELOG.md

name: Symphonia
baseline: FFmpeg libavcodec native decoders (FLAC, ALAC, MP1, MP2, MP3, AAC-LC, Vorbis, ADPCM), single-threaded, built as the static 'ffbench' example from a pdeljanov/FFmpeg fork
workload: Single-thread decode-only of one or two real audio files per codec (44.1/48/96 kHz), timed with hyperfine (30 runs after 3 warmups), on an Intel Core i7-4790K, an Apple M1 Pro and a Raspberry Pi 4B.
claimed_speedup: Relative decode time Symphonia/FFmpeg (below 1.0 means Symphonia is faster). i7-4790K: FLAC 0.71-0.74, ALAC 0.73-0.79, MP1 0.45-0.48, MP2 0.60, MP3 320 kbps 0.84, ADPCM IMA 0.83. M1 Pro: FLAC 0.51-0.64, ALAC 0.77-0.81, MP1 0.63-0.64, MP2 0.72-0.77, ADPCM MS 0.59, MP3 320 kbps 0.81. Raspberry Pi 4B: FLAC 0.96-1.04, ALAC 0.81-0.88, MP1 0.83-0.87, MP2 0.91-0.93. Slower than FFmpeg on AAC-LC (1.10-1.27), Vorbis (1.05-1.24) and MP3 128 kbps (1.00-1.07). The README summarises this as 'generally +/-15%' of FFmpeg.
compiler_and_flags: Symphonia built with rustc 1.67.0 and RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native', SIMD enabled. FFmpeg built with a plain './configure' (compiler version and flags not stated).
hardware: Intel Core i7-4790K 4C/8T @ 4.0 GHz; Apple M1 Pro (8 Firestorm + 2 Icestorm cores); Raspberry Pi 4B (Broadcom BCM2711, Cortex-A72 @ 1.5 GHz)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust audio decoding and demuxing library, no C API yet (listed as planned), so using it from C++ needs a hand-written FFI shim. Decode only, no encoders. Needs a recent rustc, and the README says performance depends strongly on compiler version because the decoders rely on auto-vectorization.
caveats: First-party results, so tier C: the test files come from the author's personal media library (not published) and only one or two files are used per codec, which the page itself says favours the decoders it was tuned on. The page was last updated 2023-02-03 (rustc 1.67.0, Symphonia main of that date), long before the current v0.6.1, so the numbers may be stale. The FFmpeg C compiler and flags are not stated. Results are mixed: Symphonia loses on AAC-LC and Vorbis everywhere and on most codecs on the Raspberry Pi, and wins mainly on FLAC, ALAC, MP1 and MP2. FFmpeg ran single-threaded (its FLAC/ALAC threading is not the default).

name: VVenC
baseline: VTM-19.2 (JVET VVC reference encoder) and HM-17.0 (HEVC reference encoder); x265 v3.5 is also plotted but only in figures
workload: Random-access encoding of JVET common-test-condition HD and UHD sequences at QP 22/27/32/37, VVenC with 8 threads, reported as encoder runtime speedup together with PSNR BD-rate versus HM-17.0.
claimed_speedup: VVenC v1.14.0 Table III (HD4K): faster preset 2400x, fast 1100x, medium 330x, slow 87x, slower 19x faster than VTM-19.2 (HD column: 2400x/1100x/280x/74x/15x); versus HM-17.0 the same presets are 380x/180x/53x/14x/3x faster with PSNR BD-rate of -13.3%/-25.8%/-35.1%/-39.1%/-42.1%. The x265 v3.5 comparison (PSNR and MS-SSIM tuned, 8 threads) appears only as figures. Page cites peer-reviewed VVenC papers that were not opened (IEEE and ACM are blocked here). name: xin26x
baseline: x265 (HEVC encoder), --preset fast, single thread
workload: Single-thread low-delay (IPPP, no B-frames) HEVC encoding at 1080p and 720p on four YUV sequences at fixed bitrates, comparing encode FPS and PSNR with x265.
claimed_speedup: README: 'The performance of xin26x(HEVC) is x4 compared to x265 under single unit core.' Table rows (xin26x FPS vs x265 FPS, PSNR in dB): BasketballDrive 1080p 20.68 vs 7.96 (36.929 vs 36.913); pedestrian_area 1080p 39.203 vs 8.35 (39.719 vs 39.707); KristenAndSara 720p 103.68 vs 23.56 (43.218 vs 43.183); sc_desktop 1080p 39.48 vs 16.83 (40.082 vs 29.817). Ratios 2.60x, 4.69x, 4.40x, 2.35x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Compiler and flags for both binaries are not stated (builds via CMake and Visual Studio 2022 on Windows). Commands: xin26x_test.exe -a 0 -I 0 --wpp 0 --thread 1 --preset 0 (preset 3 for BasketballDrive) --bframes 0; x265.exe --preset fast -I -1 --pools 1 --bframes 0 --frame-threads 0 --no-wpp --tune psnr. README says x265 is the 2020/12/25 version (stated for the offline table).
tradeoffs: Encoder framework for HEVC and VVC (AV1 is intra-frame only and unoptimised pure C). Plain C API (xin_app_enc.c shows usage). Needs x86 with AVX2; max resolution 3860x2160; max 3 temporal layers; AGPL-3.0 copyleft. Optimised for real-time communication, so it lacks some offline tools (the README says lookahead and cu-tree were enabled for fairness in the offline comparison).
caveats: First-party table only; CPU model is not stated and the test sequences are not in the repo (only a Google Drive link to output bitstreams). xin26x presets differ per sequence (preset 3 for one, preset 0 for the rest), so the settings are not matched to x265 fast beyond similar PSNR. x265 build is from 2020-12-25, long out of date. The sc_desktop row is not like for like (xin26x used a screen-content tool, PSNR 40.082 versus 29.817 for x265). README also shows a BD-rate table against x265 veryslow that was not examined for speed. Repo history starts 2026-04 per the commits page.
found_via: Not an HN thread. Hacker News pass was thin; found on github.com/topics/video-codec (sorted by stars) while following up HN leads, then opened the README

name: rav1e
baseline: libaom (AV1 reference encoder)
workload: AV1 video encoding speed; the README positions rav1e for cases where libaom is too slow, with speed presets 0-10.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'The fastest and safest AV1 encoder.' and 'in its current form it is most suitable for cases where libaom (the reference encoder) is too slow.'
tradeoffs: Written in Rust with hand-written x86_64 NASM and NEON assembly; needs NASM 2.14.02 or newer and Rust 1.85 or newer. A C API can be built (README section 'Building the C-API'), so it is callable from C++. 11 speed settings from exhaustive to near real-time.
caveats: The README gives no benchmark. The HN thread snippet 'The fastest and safest AV1 encoder but it's also 62.1% assembly?' questions the claim, and other AV1 encoders such as SVT-AV1 are commonly reported as faster; I did not verify that here. Report as tier D only because the project is notable. A verifier should find a public benchmark (for example Phoronix or AOM Codec Working Group tests) or retier it.
